title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF ACCOUNTING: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES FOR EMERGING ECONOMIES
summary: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies is transforming the accounting and financial reporting environment. Traditional accounting processes increasingly rely on automated data processing, machine learning, intelligent document recognition, predictive analytics, and digital financial reporting systems. These technologies create opportunities to improve the efficiency, accuracy, transparency, and timeliness of accounting information. At the same time, the adoption of AI introduces new challenges related to data quality, cybersecurity, professional competence, ethical responsibility, explainability, and regulatory oversight. This study examines the opportunities and challenges associated with the application of artificial intelligence in accounting, with particular attention to emerging economies. The research applies a qualitative review-based methodology and analyses academic literature, professional publications, and international developments in digital financial reporting. The findings indicate that AI can significantly reduce repetitive accounting tasks, support financial analysis, improve fraud detection, and enhance the accessibility of financial information. However, technological adoption alone does not guarantee high- high-quality accounting outcomes. The effectiveness of AI depends on data quality, appropriate governance mechanisms, professional judgement, digital skills, and institutional readiness. The study argues that emerging economies should adopt a balanced human–AI approach in which artificial intelligence supports, rather than replaces, professional accounting judgement. The paper concludes by proposing key directions for responsible AI adoption in accounting, including professional education, data governance, cybersecurity, regulatory development, and continuous human oversight. title: Decoding Blockchain Adoption: A UTAUT and PLS-SEM Analysis of IT Practitioners' Behavioral Intention in Nepal's Emerging Digital Economy
summary: Background: Blockchain’s secure, decentralized design extends beyond cryptocurrencies, but integration and trust issues limit adoption. IT practitioners play a key role in its implementation. This study examines factors influencing blockchain adoption in Kathmandu Valley using the UTAUT framework. Purpose: The purpose of this study is to examine IT practitioners’ behavioral intention toward blockchain adoption in Kathmandu Valley. Design/methodology/approach: A Causal-Comparative design with a sample size of 407 IT Practitioners drawn from the purposive random sampling of Kathmandu Valley is undertaken. Data was analyzed by employing descriptive and inferential statistics along with SEM. Findings: The findings reveal that Performance Expectancy (β = 0.177, p = 0.011), Effort Expectancy (β = 0.283, p < 0.001), Social Influence (β = 0.170, p = 0.041), and Facilitating Conditions (β = 0.184, p = 0.001) significantly influence IT practitioners’ behavioral intention (BI) toward blockchain adoption, with BI strongly predicting Use Behavior (β = 0.699, p < 0.001). Mediation analysis further shows that BI significantly mediates the effects of these factors on Use Behavior, highlighting its central role in translating perceptions and enabling conditions into actual blockchain usage. Conclusion: IT practitioners perceive the potential of blockchain, but technical knowledge gaps and security as well as scalability issues create an impediment in its adoption. Therefore, for its broader usage, it requires training, better infrastructure, and security measures.

title: INTELLECTUAL CAPITAL AND CAPITAL STRUCTURE ON BUSINESS PERFORMANCE : THE MODERATING ROLE OF GOOD CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
summary: Food and beverage sub-sector companies in Indonesia face challenges in maintaining business performance amid increasing competition, rising production costs, and unstable economic conditions. Business performance measured using Return on Equity (ROE) experienced fluctuations and tended to decline during the 2021–2024 period. In addition, the effectiveness of intellectual capital management and capital structure policies is considered important in supporting company performance sustainability. Good Corporate Governance (GCG) is also believed to strengthen company management effectiveness and improve stakeholder trust. This study aims to analyze the effect of intellectual capital and capital structure on business performance with Good Corporate Governance as a moderating variable. This study uses a quantitative approach with associative research type. The data used are secondary data obtained from annual reports and financial statements of food and beverage sub-sector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the 2021–2024 period. The sampling technique used purposive sampling. Data analysis was conducted using panel data regression and Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA) through EViews 10 software. The results show that intellectual capital and capital structure do not significantly affect business performance. Furthermore, Good Corporate Governance is unable to moderate the relationship between intellectual capital and business performance as well as the relationship between capital structure and business performance. These findings indicate that the implementation of intellectual capital management, capital structure policy, and corporate governance has not been fully effective in improving company performance. Companies are advised to optimize internal resource management, improve operational efficiency, maintain balanced financing policies, and strengthen the implementation of corporate governance to improve business performance sustainably.

title: Dynamic connectedness between ESG and sectoral stock markets in China: evidence from a quantile connectedness approach
summary: This study applies the quantile connectedness approach to evaluate the linkages between ESG and sectoral stock markets in China within a network system. The findings reveal that the system exhibits strong connectedness under the impact of specific events. Under moderate market conditions, ESG300, Financial, Consumer Discretionary, and Materials predominantly act as net transmitters, while Consumer Staples, Energy, Real Estate, Healthcare, and Utilities persist as net recipients. Industrial and Telecom undergo connectedness shifts due to pivotal events. Moreover, under extreme market conditions, markets alternate between net receiving and net transmitting states.

title: Does State Ownership Undermine the Environmental Payoff of Corporate Green Investment? Evidence from China’s Listed Manufacturing Firms
summary: Against the backdrop of China’s dual-carbon strategy, a growing literature documents that corporate green investment improves financial outcomes, yet whether it produces genuine environmental improvement remains contested. This study shifts the analytical lens from financial to ecological returns: drawing on a panel of Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms over 2014–2023, we examine how green investment affects corporate environmental performance—proxied by the Environmental (E) pillar of ESG ratings—and whether state-owned shareholding moderates this relationship. To address endogeneity and unobserved heterogeneity, we estimate a dynamic panel model via two-step difference GMM. The results show that green investment significantly raises environmental performance, but that state ownership attenuates this effect. We interpret the main effect as operating through direct pollution and resource-use reduction, lower regulatory-compliance risk, and improved environmental disclosure, whereas in state-owned enterprises institutional frictions—political multi-tasking, soft budget constraints, and weak environmental accountability—convert green capital into largely symbolic compliance, diluting its marginal environmental return. By recentring the analysis on an independent, third-party environmental measure that blends substantive environmental outcomes with the quality of environmental disclosure, this study examines the ecological efficacy of green investment and shows that ownership structure conditions not only profitability but also the realisation of environmental benefits. Robustness checks based on alternative estimators, lagged green investment, panel unit-root tests, and expanded GMM diagnostics corroborate the core positive effect of green investment; by contrast, an objective patent-based outcome does not respond to green investment within the sample window, indicating that disclosure-based and innovation-based measures of environmental performance capture distinct margins. These checks also clarify the conditions under which the moderating role of state ownership is statistically significant.

title: REAL ESTATE INVESTMENT DECISION-MAKING CHALLENGES AMONG GOVERNMENT-LINKED INVESTMENT COMPANIES IN MALAYSIA
summary: Institutional real estate investment decisions in emerging economies remain underexplored, particularly among government-linked entities that must balance commercial returns with broader national development mandates. Although Malaysia government-linked investment companies (GLICs) are among the country’s dominant institutional investors in the commercial real estate market, the challenges influencing their real estate investment decisions remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the challenges that influence real estate investment decisions among Malaysian GLICs. A qualitative study design was adopted, drawing on semi-structured interviews with 15 key informants directly involved in real estate investment decision-making. Thematic analysis identified challenges across two broad dimensions, namely internal and external. Internal challenges include organisational and structural constraints, behavioural biases such as herding and home bias, and social and sustainable challenges, including environmental, social, and governance (ESG) pressure and ambitious development. External challenges comprise political and geopolitical risk, macroeconomic challenges, real estate market constraints, and regulatory and legal requirements. These findings reveal a dual mandate tension between achieving risk-adjusted returns and fulfilling socio-political obligations. This study contributes to the limited literature on institutional real estate investment challenges in emerging economies and offers practical implications for fund managers, policymakers, and regulators seeking to enhance institutional real estate investment practices in Malaysia.

title: Digital Transformation and Low-Carbon Transition Risk in Manufacturing Firms: A Green Innovation Perspective
summary: Promoting the digital transformation of manufacturing and reducing the risks of the low-carbon transition are necessary steps to achieve carbon peaking and neutrality goals and drive all-round green development. Using publicly listed manufacturing enterprises in China from 2010 to 2024 as the research sample, this paper empirically examines the effect of digital transformation on corporate vulnerability to low-carbon transition and identifies the corresponding transmission paths. Digital transformation will reduce the risk of the low-carbon transition for manufacturing companies. Green innovation provides a necessary path for digital transformation to mitigate the aforementioned risk. After adding another category to the classification of innovation drivers, this study found that substantive green innovation significantly mediated the effect, but strategic green innovation did not. Therefore, digital transformation is likely to drive high-quality substantive changes rather than a large number of symbolic ones. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the risk-reducing effect of digital transformation is more pronounced in companies with a higher proportion of skilled technical staff, chair–CEO separation and those facing looser financing constraints. The above results provide empirical support and policy references for promoting the synchronous digital-green development of manufacturing enterprises and for identifying and mitigating low-carbon transition risks.

title: Strategic ambiguity as managerial practice: dynamic managerial capabilities and performance under digital transformation
summary: Purpose The managers working in volatile environments face an apparent paradox: coordination requires concise instructions and effective adaptation requires flexibility. In this paper, the authors introduce the concept of strategic ambiguity (SA) as a managerial intention that influences decision-making in uncertain situations. It analyzes the mediating indirect correlation between SA and firm performance by introducing dynamic managerial capabilities (DMCs) and analyzes digital transformation (DT) as a situational moderator. Design/methodology/approach The empirical test is conducted through a moderated mediation model tested using survey data collected from 393 Jordanian manufacturing small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), where analysis is done using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings Strategic ambiguity and DMCs are positively associated with each other and with firm performance. The SA-performance relationship has DMCs as its transmission mechanism. The DMC-performance connection is enhanced in digital transformation, thus acting as a situational amplifier, but not as a driver. The informal coordination practices explain how ambiguity is realized within the weak institutional setting of the emerging market conditions. Originality/value The research reconceptualizes strategic ambiguity as a choice by a manager and not a failure in communication. It builds on the body of existing literature on the topic of ambiguity tolerance by showing how ambiguity can lead to the activation of capability and clarifying the circumstances in which digital transformation can increase the effectiveness of managers in emerging-market SMEs.

title: The Accountability Pathway: Linking ESG Disclosure, Integrated Reporting Quality, and Value Creation in Southeast Asia
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines how listed firms in Southeast Asia translate internal environmental, social, and governance (ESG) commitments into accountable practices, transparent reporting, and organizational value creation. Focusing on firms in the ASEAN‐6 countries over the period 2020–2024, the study proposes and empirically tests a framework in which ESG disclosure enhances integrated reporting quality and, ultimately, value creation, as measured by investment efficiency, while accounting for macro‐level energy transition pressures and firm‐level corporate governance mechanisms. Using panel data from 2605 firms, the study employs maximum likelihood structural equation modeling within a moderated mediation framework, while controlling for country‐level fixed effects. The findings indicate that ESG disclosure significantly enhances integrated reporting quality and that reporting quality serves as a key mechanism through which ESG disclosure contributes to value creation. The results further demonstrate that the accountability pathway is context‐dependent: energy transition pressures strengthen the importance of sustainability accountability, whereas corporate governance influences firms' capacity to implement ESG strategies effectively. This study contributes to the literature by conceptualizing corporate social responsibility as a multistage process that links ESG knowledge, disclosure and reporting infrastructure, and value creation. The findings offer practical implications for managers, investors, and policymakers seeking to enhance corporate transparency and promote sustainable capital allocation across ASEAN economies.

title: Does the Clean Air Action Mitigate Upward Pressure on Debt Financing Costs? New Evidence from High-Carbon Firms in China
summary: Against the backdrop of increasingly stringent environmental governance and the growing incorporation of environmental risks into credit pricing, this study uses firm-level data from the China Tax Survey Database for 2009–2016 and employs a multi-period difference-in-differences model to examine the effect of the Clean Air Action (CAA) on debt financing costs (DFC). The results show that the CAA significantly reduces the DFC of high-carbon firms. This finding remains robust to instrumental-variable estimation, sensitivity analysis of omitted-variable bias, CS-DID estimation, and a battery of robustness checks. The effect is concentrated among small and medium-sized enterprises, private firms, and firms in the chemical industry. Reduced dependence on government support serves as a partial channel through which the CAA improves debt financing conditions. However, the policy-induced increase in reliance on short-term financing intensifies refinancing pressure and liquidity risk, partially offsetting these financing benefits. Green innovation capabilities and pre-policy cash-based debt-servicing capacity further strengthen the negative effect of the CAA on DFC. These findings extend the literature on the financial consequences of environmental policy and provide micro-level evidence on how credit allocation can support the green transition of carbon-intensive firms in emerging markets.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AND SUSTAINABILITY STRATEGIES IN THE INDONESIAN COSMETICS INDUSTRY: PORTER’S FIVE FORCES OF COMPETITIVE DYNAMICS AND GROWTH OPPORTUNITIES
summary: This article provides an overview of the analysis of the cosmetics and personal care industry in Indonesia. The cosmetics industry in Indonesia is growing rapidly in line with increasing public awareness of self-care, changes in lifestyle, and the advancement of digitalization. The presence of social media and e-commerce has also influenced consumer patterns, particularly among the younger generation, who constitute the primary market in this industry. The research method employs a qualitative descriptive approach using secondary data analysis sourced from industry reports, academic publications, and various references related to the development of the cosmetics industry in Indonesia. In analyzing the cosmetics industry, the Porter’s Five Forces model was applied, encompassing buyer power, supplier power, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitute products, and the level of competition among firms. Additionally, macro-environmental analysis was employed to understand external factors influencing the industry. The results of the analysis indicate that this industry has a high level of attractiveness with significant market opportunities; however, it also faces intense competition, low consumer loyalty, and a reliance on imported raw materials. Therefore, companies need to prioritize innovation, digital strategies, and brand strengthening to maintain their competitiveness.

title: Assessing digital literacy among Vietnamese university students: implications for educational management in the digital transformation era
summary: Purpose This study aims to assess the current state of digital literacy (DL) among Vietnamese university students in the context of digital transformation. The findings provide a foundation for recommending strategies for higher education institutions and academic libraries to enhance students' DL. Design/methodology/approach The study employed a self-assessment survey with 1,154 students selected through convenience sampling combined with purposive elements. The measurement scale was developed based on UNESCO's Digital Literacy Framework (2018) and the Jisc Digital Capabilities Framework (2024). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics. Findings Results show that students' DL is at a high level, with the highest scores observed in basic skills such as device-software operation, information handling, and digital communication. More advanced skills – including digital content creation, digital learning skills, and career-related digital competencies – were rated lower. Male students reported higher scores in technical skills, whereas female students reported higher scores in creativity and learning-related skills. Students in Education and Pedagogy reported the highest levels of DL. Third-year students reported the highest DL scores. DL scores differed across daily Internet-use groups, but the pattern was not linear. Originality/value This study provides large-scale empirical evidence on DL among Vietnamese university students, integrating internationally recognised frameworks adapted to the local educational context. The findings highlight the multidimensional nature of DL and underscore the critical role of higher education institutions and academic libraries in fostering targeted digital skill development for students. title: In search of transformative resilience in manufacturing supply chains: how and when digital platform capabilities and supply chain knowledge matter
summary: Purpose While recent Industry 5.0 paradigms emphasize human-centric and resilient manufacturing ecosystems supported by emerging technologies, the factors driving supply chain metaverse adoption (SCMA) and its mechanisms for enhancing transformative resilience remain underexplored. Unlike adaptive resilience, which focuses on recovery to pre-disruption states, transformative resilience involves fundamental reconfiguration enabling firms to emerge stronger from disruptions. Grounded in resource orchestration theory, this study examines how manufacturing firms combine digital platform capabilities (integration and reconstruction) and supply chain knowledge to drive SCMA and enhance transformative resilience. We investigate the mediating role of SCMA and the moderating effect of supply chain knowledge orchestration on the SCMA-resilience relationship. Design/methodology/approach We collected data from 300 senior managers across Ghanaian manufacturing firms using a two-wave survey design. Analysis of Moment Structures-based covariance structural equation modelingwas employed due to its suitability for theory-testing with well-established constructs, superior handling of measurement error, and ability to provide rigorous goodness-of-fit assessment. Hierarchical regression analysis examined the moderating effects. Common method bias was addressed through temporal separation, procedural remedies, and statistical tests (Harman’s single-factor test and the marker variable technique). Findings Both digital platform integration capability and reconstruction capability significantly drive SCMA. SCMA demonstrates substantial effects on transformative resilience, with effect sizes indicating strong practical significance beyond statistical significance. SCMA partially mediates the relationship between digital platform capabilities and transformative resilience. Critically, supply chain knowledge orchestration significantly strengthens the SCMA-resilience relationship, explaining an additional 12% of the variance, demonstrating that technology adoption alone is insufficient without knowledge-based capability development. Practical implications Manufacturing firms should adopt phased metaverse implementation strategies, first strengthening digital platform capabilities before full-scale deployment. Organizations must simultaneously develop knowledge orchestration mechanisms (establishing cross-functional learning structures, systematic knowledge capture processes, and virtual-to-physical translation capabilities) to maximize resilience benefits from metaverse investments. Originality/value This study advances supply chain resilience literature by demonstrating how metaverse technologies enable transformative (not merely adaptive) resilience through resource orchestration mechanisms. It extends Industry 5.0 scholarship by empirically validating the criticality of human-centric knowledge orchestration in amplifying advanced technology benefits. By revealing the conditional nature of metaverse value creation, the study provides novel theoretical insights into when and why digital platforms generate transformative outcomes, contributing to resource orchestration theory and digital transformation literature. The developing economy context offers rare empirical evidence of advanced technology adoption under resource constraints.

title: Financial, innovation and fiscal drivers of ecological efficiency across Western and Eastern European Union member states
summary: Abstract This study quantifies how green finance, financial development, green technology innovation efficiency and environmental taxes shape ecological efficiency in the European Union, and tests whether these effects differ between Western and Eastern member states. The sample covers all 27 member states over 2000–2023, giving 648 country-year observations. Ecological efficiency is measured by a dynamic slack-based measure model that treats reused water and waste incinerated for energy recovery as carry-overs, and green technology innovation efficiency by a slack-based measure model. The second-stage model regresses the logarithm of ecological efficiency on the logarithms of the four drivers, controlling for trade openness, industrial structure, human development and urbanization, and is estimated by feasible generalized least squares; robustness is assessed by system generalized method of moments, censored and bootstrapped truncated regressions, estimators robust to cross-sectional dependence, and specifications without controls. Mean ecological efficiency is 0.790, with Luxembourg, Germany and Italy highest and Bulgaria, Slovakia and Hungary lowest, and Eastern scores remain persistently below Western scores. Green finance, financial development and environmental taxes raise ecological efficiency in the full sample and in the West, whereas in the East these effects are statistically indistinguishable from zero and green technology innovation efficiency is negative. Policy should therefore be differentiated: the West should scale green bond markets and raise carbon prices, while the East should redirect cohesion funds into green investment banks, phase environmental taxes with revenue recycling, and finance technology transfer and green skills so that innovation inputs are converted into measurable efficiency gains.

title: Unstacking India stack: evolution, architecture, and FinTech transformation through digital public infrastructure—a review and future research agendas
summary: Purpose This paper aims to review India’s digital public infrastructure (DPI) and its role in shaping the broader financial technology (FinTech) ecosystem. The study synthesizes existing research, identifies key recurring themes, and examines how these themes interact within digital systems. In addition, it assesses the conceptual and empirical rigour and identifies future research directions within the DPI-FinTech domain. Design/methodology/approach The review adopts the theories, contexts, and methods (TCM) framework to organize prior studies. Thematic analysis is conducted to extract recurring patterns across the literature. To clarify overlaps among identified themes, a Venn mapping approach is used to identify the interconnections among key dimensions of DPI. The preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) protocol governs the search, screening, eligibility, and inclusion stages. A total of 63 peer-reviewed articles, indexed in Scopus and Web of Science (WoS) between 2014 and 2025, are included. Findings Four dominant themes are identified: (i) digital infrastructure, (ii) FinTech innovation, (iii) financial inclusion, and (iv) governance. The findings show that DPI operates as a socio-economic ecosystem in which the integration of infrastructure, innovation, user behaviour and regulatory frameworks shapes outcomes. While DPI has enabled rapid financial access and innovation, issues such as the digital divide, data governance, trust, and unequal adoption persist. Practical implications The synthesis offers actionable insights for policymakers and FinTech developers (FinTech Devs) by highlighting strengths and unresolved challenges within India’s DPI ecosystem. The findings can inform better design choices, governance frameworks, and targeted policy interventions. Originality/value The study makes four original contributions to the literature. First, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, it is among the first studies to systematically combine the TCM framework with thematic intersection analysis to explain the interconnected nature of the DPI-FinTech ecosystem. Second, it provides an integrated Venn mapping framework showing how the themes interact. Third, it combines the PRISMA approach with the TCM framework, backed by a systematic coding scheme. Fourth, it identifies new research areas to broaden the scope of existing DPI-FinTech research.

title: Sharpening bordering: What counts, where it operates, and what endures
summary: We respond to Laine's account of supply chains as bordering infrastructures by asking three linked questions: What counts as bordering, where does it operate, and what forms endure? We argue that bordering: (1) depends on identifiable mechanisms that differentially organize mobility; (2) operates at the intersection of territorial authority and networked infrastructure; and (3) may leave capacities that outlast particular practices. This argument extends to the post-pandemic era, where bordering capacities are strategically hardening under geopolitical, economic, and environmental instability.

title: Differential Game Analysis of Green Financing Mode in Dual Capital‐Constrained Supply Chains: The Impact of Integrating Blockchain Technology
summary: ABSTRACT Capital‐constrained low‐carbon manufacturers can choose between guarantee credit financing (GCF) and mixed financing (MF). The lack of transparency in financing information makes blockchain technology (BT) a promising solution to traditional financing challenges. How to introduce BT and make financing decisions has become a pressing challenge. This paper comprehensively considers the two financing modes of GCF and MF, and the introduction of BT or not, and constructs differential game models under four scenarios. The feedback dynamic equilibrium strategies of all members in each scenario are obtained, and BT introduction strategy and the financing mode selection in the capital‐constrained low‐carbon supply chain (CC‐LCSC) are explored. The results show that not only higher initial emissions and carbon prices but also baseline bankruptcy risk assessment coefficient and usage cost of BT suppress the CER efforts, total carbon emissions, and profits. In the same financing mode, whether introducing BT can bring better economic and environmental performance depends on the consumer green trust and usage cost of BT. In different financing modes, the MF mode can achieve “reducing emissions through loans,” and the higher the bankruptcy risk assessment correction coefficient, the more significant the advantage of introducing BT in this mode. Under conditions of moderate bankruptcy risk assessment correction coefficient and usage cost of BT, elevated consumer green trust enhances the superiority of the MF mode under the scenario with BT in achieving optimal profits and CER efforts, though it does not yield the lowest total carbon emissions.

title: Firm-Level Digital and Sustainability Indicators and Sustainability Outcomes: Evidence from Chinese Listed Industrial Firms under Environmental Regulation
summary: This study examined the associations between digital and organizational capabilities and sustainability outcomes among 200 industrial firms listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in China from 2013 to 2023. The study applied the theory of Dynamic Capabilities and Institutional Theory to explore the digital transformation, corporate sustainability culture, cultural capital and digital media literacy, and their relationship with environmental performance and sustainability innovation. Media coverage intensity and the financial support of sustainability initiatives were investigated as possible indirect pathways and environmental regulation as a moderating institutional condition. Firm and year fixed-effects models were supplemented with dynamic System GMM and bootstrapped indirect-effect analysis, moderation analysis, and robustness specifications. The findings indicate that digital transformation, corporate sustainability culture, and digital media literacy were positively associated with both environmental performance and sustainability innovation, whereas cultural capital was positively associated with sustainability innovation but not environmental performance. Media coverage intensity and financial support for sustainability initiatives showed statistically supported indirect associations for digital transformation, corporate sustainability culture, and digital media literacy, but not cultural capital. Environmental regulation generally strengthened the positive capability–sustainability associations, while its negative interaction with cultural capital for sustainability innovation provided only tentative evidence of a weakening association, as the interaction was significant only at the 10% level. These findings contribute to the Dynamic Capabilities Theory by bringing into focus capability-specific sustainability associations and the Institutional Theory by establishing differentiated regulatory conditions. The indirect effects and relationships estimated are therefore viewed as associative in nature for the purpose of the observational panel design.

title: Does good governance moderate the relationship between CEO overconfidence and corporate environmental disclosure? International evidence
summary: Purpose This paper aimed to shed light on the relationship between managerial overconfidence and corporate environmental disclosure and whether this relationship is moderated by good governance. Design/methodology/approach The sample includes 1395 international firms listed on the ESG index for the period 2010–2023. The feasible generalized least squares regression method is used to estimate the econometric models. Findings The findings reveal that CEO overconfidence promotes corporate environmental disclosure and strong governance enhances both disclosure and the impact of overconfidence, underscoring its key oversight function. Research limitations/implications The study highlights the interplay between CEO overconfidence and governance quality in shaping corporate environmental disclosure, offering a foundation for future research into the behavioral factors influencing nonfinancial reporting. Practical implications The findings indicate that CEO overconfidence increases environmental disclosure under strong governance, highlighting the need for boards, investors and policymakers to integrate executive behavioral traits with governance mechanisms to enhance ESG transparency and sustainable decision-making. Social implications The findings have societal implications by supporting greater transparency and accountability in corporate environmental disclosure, which can enhance public trust, inform climate-related decision-making and contribute to broader sustainability goals. Originality/value This study addresses a clear gap in the literature by reconciling inconclusive findings on the relationship between CEO overconfidence and environmental disclosure. Prior research has largely overlooked the moderating role of corporate governance and has treated environmental disclosure in a fragmented manner (e.g. voluntary vs mandatory). This study offers an integrated perspective by jointly examining these relationships in an international context and by conceptualizing environmental disclosure as a unified construct.

title: Corporate Governance Architecture, Ownership Structure, Institutional Context, and Financial Performance
summary: This paper examines the relationship between corporate governance, ownership structure and financial performance by synthesizing recent empirical evidence on board architecture, ownership concentration, family control, institutional investors, foreign ownership and integrated governance configurations. The literature indicates that governance mechanisms rarely produce uniform financial consequences across firms and countries. Board independence, gender diversity, leadership structure, audit committees and board size can strengthen monitoring, advisory capacity and investor confidence, but their effectiveness depends on institutional conditions, ownership distribution and organizational characteristics. Ownership concentration can reduce managerial agency problems while simultaneously increasing the risk of controlling-shareholder entrenchment. Family, institutional, foreign and state ownership similarly generate heterogeneous effects according to shareholder incentives, governance quality and economic conditions. Cross-country and emerging-market evidence further demonstrates that formal governance reforms do not automatically translate into stronger corporate outcomes unless they modify actual monitoring capacity, managerial incentives and control structures. The overall literature therefore supports a contingent interpretation of governance-performance relationships in which financial outcomes emerge from interactions among board structures, ownership characteristics, institutional environments and firm-specific conditions rather than from isolated governance mechanisms.

title: When and How Firms Can Promote Green Innovation for Sustainable Development: A Holistic Examination
summary: Green finance has become a key instrument for addressing environmental degradation and supporting sustainable development. However, existing literature has largely focused on its outcomes, with limited attention to the factors that contribute to its effectiveness. Using an input-oriented perspective, this study examines the roles of green innovation, financial development, and research and development (R&D) in promoting green financing and sustainable development. Empirical data from thirty-nine manufacturing companies in Saudi Arabia covering 2011–2025 are analyzed using partial least squares, generalized method of moments, fixed-effects, and random-effects models. The findings demonstrate that green innovation, financial development, and R&D significantly contribute to the effectiveness of green financing. The transition from conventional product innovation to green finance is found to be less challenging than the development of eco-friendly technological innovations, as environmentally friendly products can generate positive financial returns. The study provides policy insights for promoting sustainable industrial growth.

title: Young people and the data gaze: experiencing datafication in everyday life
summary: Young people’s capacity to see and know themselves is increasingly informed by algorithmic and classificatory logics. In this article, we extend Beer’s concept of the data gaze, drawing from qualitative empirical examples to illustrate how young people navigate and incorporate datafied ways of seeing and knowing in their everyday practices via engagement with financial technology (fintech) and photo editing apps. We argue that whilst young people are increasingly ‘gazed upon’ in their interactions with fintech and image-editing apps, that is, categorised and imagined by algorithmic and machinic processes, they also gaze back. We explore two specific aspects of the broader data gaze: (1) datafied money and the financialised gaze that young people experience when being nudged while using gamified fintech services, and (2) datafied bodies and the forensic gaze young people use to inform selfie-editing practices through digital ‘corrections’ to their faces and bodies. The implications of these ever-finer capacities for predictive classificatory processes are essential for understanding how life feels under the gaze of the data industry, and how inequalities and exclusions are made, automated and remade in contemporary datafied lives.

title: Monsters of finance
summary: Abstract An anthropology of horror can serve as a vernacular critique of financial speculation. Drawing on fieldwork in San Pedro, Paraguay, I track horror across three registers: pombero tricksters; plata yvyguy (buried money) as a founding myth of postwar finance; and obligations binding sesame farmers to monsters, patrones , and creditors. Horror—a critical ontology and distinctive wonder—arises when obligation becomes undecidable: when one cannot tell whether the forces manipulating time and the future are persons who stand in relation, or how far the liability extends. Paraguay has produced this condition twice, first under the Stroessner dictatorship (1954–89), with its network of civilian informants, and later under climate finance running through the same clientelist orders. As Martha Blache's 1982 study of Guarani folklore helps us understand, finance bears rather than subsumes the moral arrangements of prestation, and horror is a native theorization of speculation rather than a response to an external capitalist threat.

title: Nocturnal rewilding on a Luminous Planet: The politics of urban illumination as infrastructure ecology
summary: With the increasing recognition of nocturnal illumination as an environmental and endocrine disruptor, the night is emerging as a contested socio-ecological terrain of governance, characterised by efforts to conserve, restore and preserve darkness by a range of actors, including municipal and regional authorities, state agencies, as well as NGOs and citizen-led initiatives. Recognising the imaginary of restoring darkness as a pre-urbicene environmental condition that drives these efforts to control and regulate the night, we term this emerging paradigm of environmental governance nocturnal rewilding . Drawing upon semi-structured and walking interviews with over 30 experts, participant observation at public and professional events concerning nocturnal environments, and an analysis of policy documents and planning frameworks in Switzerland, we conceptualise nocturnal rewilding as an evolving socio-ecological process, in which darkness is actively produced through the interplay of several technical strategies. We sketch the contours of this emerging paradigm by identifying darkness zoning, intermittency and algorithmic modulation as three key strategies of this mode of environmental governance. Recognising the limitations of these strategies and possible socio-environmental injustices they produce, we argue that the governance of the night must move beyond approaches that reify binaries of light and darkness across space and time, towards post-conservation, post-restoration paradigms grounded in relational and situated practices of negotiation, attunement to multispecies infrastructure ecologies and adaptive governance. Drawing on our empirical material, we show how these practices reconfigure the infrastructure ecologies of urban illumination, enabling more ecologically attuned and context-sensitive forms of nocturnal environmental governance instead of conservation- and restoration-oriented approaches that reproduce fortress conservation paradigms reproducing nature-culture separation.

title: AI readiness and digital pedagogical competence as enablers of innovations in environmental management within higher education institutions: evidence from Vietnam
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and digital pedagogical competence (DPC) are associated with lecturers’ perceptions of digital environmental governance innovation (DEGI) and perceived environmental performance in higher education institutions (HEIs). Moving beyond isolated green technologies, the study adopts a governance-oriented perspective to explain how individual digital capabilities among academic staff are linked to perceived sustainability-related outcomes through digitally enabled environmental governance innovation. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 1,525 academic staff working in Vietnamese HEIs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was used to test the proposed capability–governance–perception framework and to examine both direct and indirect relationships among the constructs. Findings The findings indicate that AI readiness (artificial intelligence readiness) is positively associated with DPC and lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI. DPC is also positively associated with governance innovation. Most importantly, lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI are strongly associated with perceived environmental performance and indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AIR and perceived environmental outcomes within the specified model. Research limitations/implications This study is based on cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from a single national context, which limits causal inference and statistical generalisability. The findings should therefore be interpreted as perception-based associations rather than evidence of objectively measured institutional environmental improvement. Future research could adopt longitudinal, comparative, multi-source or objective-indicator designs. Practical implications The findings suggest that HEIs should move beyond technology adoption alone and invest in human digital capabilities, sustainability dashboards, environmental data reporting systems and governance structures. Strengthening AIR and DPC among academic staff may support digitally mediated governance innovations for environmental management. Social implications By highlighting governance innovation as a perception-based pathway linking digital capabilities to perceived environmental performance, this study offers insights for HEIs seeking to strengthen their sustainability responsibilities. Digitally enabled environmental governance may support broader sustainability transitions, provided it is embedded within accountable institutional practices. Originality/value This study offers empirical evidence linking individual digital capabilities to perceived environmental management outcomes in higher education through governance innovation. It extends sustainability and digital transformation research by positioning AIR and DPC as enablers of perceived digitally driven environmental governance, particularly within a Global South context.

title: Flight to Safety or Flight from Carry?
summary: We examine the distinction between safe-haven and funding currencies during market stress, focusing on how global institutional investors reallocate across currencies in crises. Using foreign exchange forward and sovereign bond flows from a major custodian bank, we find that although the Swiss franc, Japanese yen, and US dollar often attract inflows in turbulent periods, their roles differ. The US dollar drew inflows during the Global Financial Crisis and geopolitical events, while the 2024 carry unwind led to elevated inflows into the Japanese yen. We develop a panel regression framework to classify crises as flights to safety or from carry. Around Liberation Day, carry dynamics dominated safety. Distinguishing carry- from safety-driven flows became more important as US rates rose in late 2022.

title: ESG performance, analysts’ forecast accuracy and board gender diversity: international evidence
summary: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG) ratings are associated with analysts’ forecast accuracy and whether board gender diversity moderates the relationship between ESG ratings and analysts’ forecast accuracy. Design/methodology/approach The sample comprises 23,498 firm-year observations across 36 countries over the period 2011–2022, with data obtained from I/B/E/S, Thomson Reuters and Refinitiv. Generalized Least Squares with panel-specific heteroskedasticity is used as the baseline estimator, with model choice supported by a Wald test. Robustness checks include fixed-effects models with clustered standard errors, propensity score matching and a Heckman selection correction. Findings ESG ratings are associated with lower analyst forecast errors when board gender diversity remains below approximately 18.5% (or 20.7% for executive-level diversity). Beyond these levels, the relationship reverses, with higher diversity associated with reduced ESG informativeness. The interaction term (+0.0097***) reflects this pattern: ESG is associated with improved accuracy on less diverse boards, has limited net effect near the threshold and is associated with reduced accuracy on more diverse boards. This non-linearity is not captured under a standard linear specification and becomes apparent only through marginal effects analysis. Practical implications For firms, the findings suggest that board diversification efforts may be more effective when undertaken prior to large-scale ESG commitments. Analysts may benefit from considering board composition when interpreting ESG ratings. Regulators may wish to consider coordinating diversity-related requirements with ESG disclosure mandates rather than addressing them independently. Originality/value This study contributes evidence of a threshold-based relationship between board diversity and ESG informativeness using cross-country data spanning 36 countries. The identified threshold of approximately 18.5% may serve as a reference point for discussions on sustainability governance standards across different national contexts.

title: Boosting Firm Value: Sustainability Report and Good Corporate Governance Moderated by Firm Size
summary: Background: Firm value has become a central concern in capital market studies, as it reflects investor confidence and long-term corporate sustainability. Prior empirical evidence on the effects of sustainability reporting (SR) and good corporate governance (GCG) on firm value remains inconclusive, warranting further investigation, particularly with respect to potential moderating factors such as firm size proxied by market capitalization. Objective: This study aims to integrate sustainability reporting and good corporate governance variables that influence firm value by using firm size as a moderating variable. Methods: This research employed a quantitative methodology utilizing a purposive sampling strategy. The participants in the study comprised 62 manufacturing firms listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange from 2021 to 2024. A cumulative total of 248 data observations were examined using SPSS software. Results: The findings of the study reveal that sustainability reporting (β = 2.981, p < 0.01), the presence of an independent board of commissioners (β = 4.275, p < 0.01), and the audit committee (β = 1.004, p < 0.01) each have a significant positive direct impact on firm value. Additionally, firm size plays a significant moderating role in the relationship between sustainability reporting and firm value (interaction β = 0.389, p < 0.05) as well as between the independent board of commissioners and firm value (interaction β = 0.421, p < 0.05). However, firm size does not moderate the relationship between audit committees and firm value (interaction β = −0.051, p > 0.05). These conclusions are drawn from a sample of 62 manufacturing firms listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) from 2021 to 2024, resulting in 248 company-year observations. Conclusion: Future research could explore other moderating variables such as profitability or apply the model in a cross-industry or cross-country context to test the robustness of these findings.

title: From Clicks to Sustainable Development: The Role of Platform Economy in Energy Transition
summary: The platform economy has reorganized urban service markets worldwide, yet its environmental implications remain insufficiently understood. We examine whether platform-economy entry affects urban energy transition, exploiting the staggered entry of food-delivery and ride-hailing platforms across 280 Chinese cities (2008–2023) as a quasi-natural experiment. Platform entry raises cities’ energy transition index by about 3%, with larger effects on current energy-system performance than on transition readiness. We provide evidence consistent with three mechanisms: capital substitution via electric-vehicle adoption, labor reallocation from energy-intensive sectors alongside induced technological upgrading, and expanded green innovation from platform-enabled time savings. Effects are stronger amid population aging, dependency burdens, and EV-charging infrastructure, but weaker in manufacturing-dependent cities—identifying a previously unrecognized environmental co-benefit of platform expansion.

title: Accuracy, Transparency, and Verifiability of Sustainability Communication in Hotel SMEs: A Comparative Analysis
summary: Introduction: This study examines the accuracy and transparency of sustainability communication among hotel SMEs. It assesses whether disclosed environmental information is generic or evidence-based and verifiable, making environmental claims more authentic. Methodology: The investigation is based on a manual textual analysis of sustainability communication published on the official websites of a sample of hotel SMEs operating in the Metropolitan City of Rome, selected as a high-intensity tourism context. Subsequently, specific indices of sustainability disclosure quality were calculated. The analysis is further complemented by an exploratory comparison of leadership structures, aimed at identifying potential differences in the quality and modes of communication between female-led and non-female-led firms. Results: The findings show that sustainability communication among the sampled hotel SMEs is generally limited, mostly symbolic, and seldom supported by verifiable evidence. Exploratory results also suggest that female-led firms display a slightly greater tendency toward formalized and verifiable environmental disclosure, though only in a few cases. Conclusion: This study contributes to the literature on sustainability communication in tourism by emphasizing not merely the presence of information but its quality, accuracy, and verifiability. The combined application of content analysis and disclosure quality indices offers a structured and replicable assessment of sustainability communication in hotel SMEs, an area that remains underexplored in the literature.

title: Upstream land-use change and transboundary river water redistribution: a global mapping
summary: Transboundary river basins sustain over three billion people across 150 + nations; however, upstream land-use and land-cover change (LULCC) remains absent from the codified text of international water treaties. In this study, we present a global, spatially explicit quantification of this governance blind spot, to our knowledge the first at treaty-comparable resolution. Using a basin-country-unit (BCU) framework spanning 313 transboundary basins, we mapped five upstream land-use transition types using MODIS satellite data (2001–2023), quantified their water consumption through climate-corrected evapotranspiration attribution, and expressed the result as a Silent Water Redistribution Index (SWRI) for all downstream territories. We find that upstream land use silently removes −31.66 km 3 yr. −1 from downstream water budgets, dominated by irrigation expansion (−36.37 km 3 yr. −1 ) and reforestation (−23.76 km 3 yr. −1 ), a signal corroborated by GRACE satellite gravity in 62% of the 13 basins in which the redistributed volume reaches at least 1% of the receiving country’s renewable water resources. Systematic comparison with water treaty records reveals that international water agreements leave 78.5% of the global signal ungoverned, exposing millions of people in downstream territories to unrecognized hydrological impacts. The reforestation paradox, wherein climate finance incentivizes upstream afforestation that reduces downstream water availability, warrants institutional attention. Our SWRI framework provides the quantitative foundation for integrating land-use governance into institutional water law.

title: Foundation first: a health-system readiness framework for responsible AI adoption in Somalia
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a mechanism for expanding access, strengthening surveillance, improving clinical decisions, and increasing health-system efficiency. Yet AI implementation is path-dependent: its value depends on the health-system, digital, institutional, and social foundations into which it is introduced. Somalia provides a critical test of this proposition because a dynamic telecommunications ecosystem coexists with uneven electricity, broadband use, primary care capacity, routine data quality, digital skills, and governance, particularly across rural, pastoralist, nomadic, displaced, and drought-affected populations. This Perspective develops a foundation-first AI implementation agenda for Somalia. It integrates the World Health Organization health-system building blocks, the Nonadoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread and Sustainability framework, and an equity lens, while aligning proposed actions with the Sustainable Development Goals, Somalia's National Transformation Plan 2025–2029, Health Sector Strategic Plan III, and African Union Agenda 2063. The central argument is that AI should be treated as a capstone of digital transformation rather than its starting point. Reliable energy, inclusive connectivity, strong primary and community care, interoperable information systems, workforce capability, sustainable financing, and accountable governance should precede or accompany AI deployment. This sequencing can convert AI from a potentially exclusionary technology into a context-fit multiplier of health-system capacity.

title: Faktor-Faktor yang Mempengaruhi Pemilihan Kantor Akuntan pada Perusahaan Perbankan
summary: This study aims to examine the effect of foreign ownership, independent commissioners, and audit committee effectiveness on the selection of Public Accounting Firms (PAFs) in banking companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) during 2020–2024. This study uses a quantitative method with secondary data obtained from companies’ annual reports. The sample was selected using purposive sampling based on predetermined criteria. The data were then analyzed using logistic regression. The results show that foreign ownership has no effect on PAF selection. Independent commissioners also have no effect on PAF selection. Meanwhile, audit committee effectiveness has a positive and significant effect on PAF selection. These results indicate that companies with more effective audit committees tend to have a greater likelihood of selecting Big Four PAFs. Therefore, audit committee effectiveness is one of the factors related to a company’s decision in selecting the PAF to be appointed

title: Is corporate social responsibility disclosure associated with stock liquidity? Evidence from Vietnam
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine whether corporate social responsibility disclosure (CSRD) is associated with stock liquidity in Vietnam’s prescribed reporting setting. Design/methodology/approach Using 2,476 firm-year observations for 499 non-financial firms during 2015–2019, the study estimates firm and year fixed-effects models with firm-clustered standard errors. CSRD is measured by score and percentage; liquidity is measured by effective and quoted spreads. First-difference and one-year-lagged specifications assess robustness. Findings Neither CSRD measure is significantly associated with either spread after firm-specific heterogeneity and common annual conditions are controlled for. The findings indicate that greater disclosure intensity alone does not necessarily reduce spread-based trading costs when reporting does not ensure comparable, credible and decision-useful information. Research limitations/implications The study is confined to Vietnamese non-financial firms within a specific timeframe. Future research could examine multiple countries, alternative liquidity measures and the credibility and investor use of disclosed information. Practical implications Firms should not assume that increasing disclosure quantity will reduce spread-based trading costs. The findings emphasize reporting comparability, consistency, assurance and enforcement. Originality/value Evidence on CSRD and stock-market liquidity remains mixed. Unlike positive findings based on externally assessed transparency, report events, global reporting initiative (GRI) adoption or mandatory reforms, this study finds no robust association for observed GRI-based disclosure intensity in Vietnam, consistent with evidence from Jordan. Disclosure volume may therefore convey a weaker market signal than standardized or salient disclosure changes.

title: Impacts of Edge AI/agentic AI on supply chain management and operations research
summary: Abstract Edge AI refers to the deployment and execution of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms on decentralized, local computing devices (e.g., Internet of Things) rather than relying on centralized cloud‐based computing infrastructures. The literature has addressed the increasing importance of AI in supply chain and operations management (SCOM), specifically in learning‐based, generative, and agentic AI, as well as digital twins. However, the area of Edge AI has not yet received a theoretical framing and conceptualization in SCOM. In this paper, we discuss the impacts of Edge AI on SCOM. We begin with an analysis of AI in SCOM, focusing on learning‐based, generative, agentic AI, and digital twins. We then detail Edge AI's impacts on SCOM across Digital SCOR functions: orchestration, fulfillment and ordering, planning, sourcing, regeneration, synchronization, and transformation. We also analyze organizational transformations that Edge AI might trigger. Specifically, we discuss interactions of agentic AI and Edge AI, an integration of local and centralized decision‐making, and deployment scenarios of Edge AI use in SCOM, focusing on production planning and control, intralogistics, and supply chain resilience. Risks and challenges of the new technology are considered as well. Impacts of Edge AI on supply chain and operations research are discussed. We conclude that Edge AI is a crucial part of the unfolding Industry 6.0 revolution that, in combination with agentic AI, provides a technology to implement decentralized, autonomously planned and controlled supply chain, production, and logistics processes, materializing in Industry 6.0 with AI across all layers of value‐added chains.

title: Aligning clean energy innovations with the SDGs: sectoral dynamics of green bonds and sustainability-enhanced equities across market conditions
summary: This study examines the dynamic interconnections among clean energy innovations, green bonds, and sectoral sustainability-enhanced equities, and their implications for advancing SDGs 7, 9, 11, 12, and 13. Using a Quantile VAR model and daily data from 31 October 2016–27 December 2024, we decompose systemic spillovers across extremely adverse (5th quantile), typical (50th quantile), and highly favourable (95th quantile) market conditions. Our results reveal a pronounced U-shaped pattern in systemic integration: the Total Connectedness Index surges to near-peak levels of approximately 89–95% at both tails, indicating that diversification benefits collapse during crises and market exuberance alike. Clean energy, green bonds, and utilities consistently act as net receivers, absorbing shocks transmitted by cyclical sectors. In contrast, industrials and consumer discretionary emerge as persistent net transmitters that drive systemic risk. Defensive sectors, notably healthcare and consumer staples, remain relatively resilient across all regimes. Importantly, green bonds, often perceived as safe-haven assets, exhibit state-dependent vulnerability to tail shocks, challenging their unconditional stabilising role. These findings imply that portfolio managers must abandon reliance on average-correlation diversification and instead adopt tail-risk-aware, dynamically allocated strategies. For regulators, the results underscore the need to integrate climate-aligned, quantile-dependent stress testing into macroprudential frameworks to safeguard financial stability during the low-carbon transition. By linking sectoral spillover dynamics to SDG outcomes, this research provides actionable guidance to enhance the resilience of sustainable finance ecosystems.Key Policy HighlightsSystemic connectedness rises to 89–95% during market stress and exuberance, sharply reducing diversification benefits.Industrial and consumer discretionary sectors are the main transmitters of shocks and should be prioritised in systemic risk monitoring.Clean energy, utilities, and green bonds primarily absorb shocks, making them vulnerable to spillovers from other sectors.Green bonds do not consistently act as safe-haven assets during extreme market conditions.Quantile-based climate stress testing and tail-risk-sensitive regulation can strengthen financial resilience and support SDGs 7, 9, 11, 12, and 13.

title: Analyzing the Key Influencing Factors of Contractors’ Environmentally Responsible Behavior in Megaprojects: A Social Network Analysis
summary: Abstract In the context of environmental governance in megaprojects, contractors’ environmentally responsible behavior (ERB) plays an increasingly critical role. Previous studies have focused primarily on identifying individual factors influencing such behavior, but they have largely overlooked the potential interrelationships among these factors. This gap may result in misjudging their actual impact. Therefore, this study examined both the interrelationships and relative importance of factors affecting contractors’ ERB in megaprojects. First, based on a literature review and the Delphi method, 20 influencing factors were identified from a stakeholder perspective. Expert surveys subsequently were conducted to quantify the interrelationships among these factors. Finally, by employing social network analysis, an influencing factor network model was constructed, and the significance of each factor was assessed. The findings reveal 13 key influencing factors and 21 critical interactions. Among these, contractual governance, ascription of responsibility, environmental awareness, and organizational culture emerge as core factors. This study enhances understanding of the complex interrelationships among influencing factors and provides practical guidance for fostering contractors’ ERB in megaprojects.

title: Sustainable accounting and its impact on business development: A systematic review
summary: This systematic literature review (SLR) examines how sustainable accounting influences business development by synthesizing evidence from 71 articles published between 2020 and 2025 and indexed in Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). The objective of this study was to analyze the influence of sustainable accounting on business development and identify the main organizational challenges, implementation strategies, and outcomes associated with its adoption. Using the PICO strategy and the PRISMA protocol, the study identifies key organizational challenges, implementation strategies, and outcomes related to sustainable accounting. The findings show that sustainable accounting strengthens business development through corporate social responsibility (CSR), sustainability reporting, environmental management accounting, technological innovation, risk management, cost efficiency, and long-term value creation. In particular, 42 percent of the reviewed studies emphasized improvements linked to social responsibility and corporate governance, while the remaining evidence highlighted financial transparency, technological innovation, and environmental accounting practices. Consistent with Schaltegger et al. (2022) and Alsarayrah et al. (2024), the review concludes that sustainable accounting is both a managerial and strategic tool for integrating economic, social, and environmental performance. The article contributes by systematizing recent evidence, identifying research gaps, and supporting the adoption of sustainable accounting practices for long-term business development.

title: FARMERS’ KNOWLEDGE, ATTITUDES AND PRACTICES ON OPEN BURNING REGULATION: A CASE STUDY OF SEKINCHAN, SELANGOR
summary: Despite a regulatory prohibition under the Environmental Quality Act 1974, open burning persists in Malaysia. Enforcement challenges are particularly evident in agricultural areas because seasonal farming cycles often involve farmers burning crop residues to clear land. Certain open burning activities, including smallholder cultivation, are permitted under specified conditions. This study explores farmers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding the regulatory controls and the local community’s perception of the issue in Sekinchan, Selangor. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the study combined quantitative surveys involving 144 respondents with qualitative interviews and field observations. The data were subsequently triangulated to enhance validity. The findings indicate that farmers have a high level of knowledge of the legal prohibition. They are also willing to participate in government awareness initiatives. However, interview and observational findings suggest that actual compliance with procedural and environmental requirements remains inconsistent. Economic considerations, time constraints, limited access to practical alternatives, and entrenched cultural norms continue to influence farmers’ behaviour. The findings indicate gaps between regulatory awareness and implementation. Therefore, integrated enforcement strategies and feasible agricultural alternatives are required to support sustainable environmental governance, agricultural land management, and context-sensitive environmental planning in Selangor.

title: Investigating green finance product awareness and perceived adoption influencers
summary: Green finance (GF) is an avenue to achieve Sustainable Development Goals and economic inclusion. While several studies have focused on GF investment instruments, such as green bonds and green funds, retail instruments, such as green mortgages and green loans, are often overlooked. South African consumers are believed to lack financial literacy; therefore, their lack of awareness of a niche concept such as GF and the limited availability of data on retail consumers and sustainable finance present a challenge. Additionally, the study of awareness separately is not enough, as it does not always translate to use. This study explored financial institutions’ employee awareness and the use of specific GF products available in the South African market, as well as perceived factors influencing personal and consumer use. Thirteen semi-structured interviews were conducted and thematically analysed. Findings showed employee awareness of all 10 products, with the Standard Bank green bond and RMB green bond highly recognised. Although awareness was high, the use of GF products was very low; only two participants used the surveyed products. The three products with actual use were for home financing, and energy-efficiency home financing was the most popular intended use. GF issuers, the structure of GF and individuals’ perceptions and beliefs about sustainability were factors influencing the use of GF products. This study provides new insights into challenges that need to be tackled to advance GF. An accessible GF market is possible through awareness and educational campaigns, by restructuring GF and GF issuers and by appealing to and addressing individual intrinsic motivators.

title: Unveiling the Antecedents of Technology‐Organization‐Environment on Low Carbon Performance: A Comparative Analysis of Emission‐Controlled and Non‐Emission‐Controlled Firms
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines firm low‐carbon performance (FLCP) by integrating the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework with the Natural Resource‐Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and Institutional Theory. Using survey data from 318 managers in Chinese firms and partial least squares structural equation modeling, it examines direct and indirect associations between TOE drivers and FLCP, plus supplementary multi‐group analysis (MGA) based on regulatory exposure and managerial awareness. Results reveal positive associations of technological competence, top management support (TMS), government support, and regulatory factors with FLCP. Financial benefits relate to FLCP indirectly through TMS, whereas government support relates directly and indirectly through TMS. The MGA results indicate that regulatory factors are stronger for firms aware of their emission‐control status, government support is stronger for unaware firms, and corporate social responsibility relates more strongly to FLCP among emission‐controlled firms. The study clarifies capability‐based TOE mechanisms and the institutional context of emerging‐economy carbon trading.
