title: Environmental Responsibility in Saudi Banking: A Stakeholder Analysis of Green Finance Adoption
summary: ABSTRACT Green finance adoption in state‐directed emerging markets remains poorly understood among stakeholder groups. This study examines how environmental responsibility and green finance are interpreted, implemented, and governed in Saudi banking. Based on 25 semi‐structured interviews across nine stakeholder categories, reflexive thematic analysis identified five themes. Stakeholders agreed that banks' environmental responsibility extends beyond operations to capital allocation, but evaluated the credibility of green finance differently depending on institutional role. National policy was perceived to legitimise organisational attention more directly within banks than among SMEs. Weak measurement architecture emerged as a credibility‐risk pathway rather than evidence of intentional greenwashing. Organisational participants described resistance as mainly practical, although commercial tensions remained. Shari'ah governance was viewed as a conditional accountability resource when linked to technical verification and substantive oversight. The study offers a bounded, multi‐stakeholder explanation of green finance adoption. Regulators should strengthen proportionate market capacity; supervisors should test governance and evidential support; and standard setters should improve definitions, KPIs, comparability, and assurance.

title: When Is ESG Performance Associated with Firm Value? The Moderating Role of Employee Turnover
summary: This study examines the relationships among ESG performance, employee turnover, and firm value and investigates whether employee turnover conditions the valuation relevance of ESG performance firms of different sizes across Taiwanese firms using data from 2019 to 2024. The study uses 10,247 firm-year observations to classify firms into smaller and larger firm-size groups using K-means clustering based solely on firm size and estimates the relationships across the full sample and the two size-based groups. The findings show that ESG and environmental performance are positively linked to firm value, especially in the larger firm-size group. Corporate governance performance is positively associated with firm value only in the larger firm-size group, while social performance shows no significant direct effect. Employee turnover is negatively associated with firm value in the larger firm-size group and conditions the ESG–firm value relationship. Moderation effects are significant among smaller firms, whereas the moderating effect of employee turnover on social performance is significant among larger firms. The study contributes to the ESG–firm value literature by incorporating employee turnover as a human-capital condition and by demonstrating a firm-size effect on ESG valuation. The findings suggest that ESG performance and workforce stability should be considered jointly when assessing the potential value implications of corporate sustainability practices.

title: The impact of market-incentive environmental policies on enterprise digital transformation: evidence from China’s carbon emissions trading pilot programmes
summary: Market-incentive environmental policies guide enterprises to proactively reduce emissions and undergo digital transformation by altering market signals and cost calculations, and are significant for the green economy. This study employs China’s carbon emissions trading pilot policy (Cpolicy) as a quasi-natural experiment. It uses a multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) model to analyze data on China’s A-share-listed enterprises (2010–2021). The results show that Cpolicy significantly drives enterprise digital transformation. This primarily stems from increases in goodwill, new investment, and innovation input and output triggered by Cpolicy. The effects of Cpolicy vary significantly across industries, firm sizes, and ownership types, underscoring the need for tailored policies. Furthermore, enterprise financial asset allocation and supply chain concentration show notable threshold effects; moderate levels of financial asset allocation and external collaboration enhance Cpolicy’s effectiveness. Overall, Cpolicy significantly stimulates enterprise digital transformation, but targeted measures are needed to maximise its impact.

title: Unequal shades of green: A human rights review of Indonesia's green finance policies
summary: Abstract Motivation Indonesia's green finance policies (GFPs) have been evolving, but questions remain about their consistency with human rights (HR) and social justice. This issue is particularly important as the green transition can generate social exclusion and uneven impacts on affected communities if environmental objectives are pursued without substantive rights‐based safeguards. Purpose This article reviews the extent to which green finance instruments, such as taxonomies and certified green actions, align with social justice as an integral part of sustainable development. It specifically assesses whether existing GFPs provide substantive safeguards against social exclusion and structural inequality beyond procedural and environmental compliance. Approach and Methods Drawing on a pragmatist paradigm, it employs desk analysis and normative juridical review to examine Indonesia's GFPs and their alignment with three dimensions of HR: the right to a clean and sustainable environment, equitable access to green finance, and protection against social and economic inequalities. The desk analysis covers academic literature, policy documents, reports, and local newspaper reports, while the normative juridical review assesses the legal status and substantive content of relevant GFP regulations. Findings The findings indicate that existing policies are primarily administrative in nature and focused on environmental classification, meeting formal legal and regulatory requirements but offering limited substantive safeguards against social exclusion and structural inequality affecting local communities. Persistent gaps between the regulatory framework and on‐the‐ground implementation result in divergence from the sustainability principle of “Do no significant harm.” Policy Implications The review highlights the risks of social exclusion and structural inequality in the green transition, underscoring the need for an HR‐based regulatory framework. Beyond Indonesia, it also highlights how prioritizing proceduralism to secure public legitimacy while sidelining instrumentalism may erode social justice. It also extends the literature on GFP and sustainability by foregrounding how regulatory proceduralism may obscure rights‐based accountability, a dimension underexplored in global GF discourses.

title: ASSESSMENT OF ESG REPORTING AMONG MONGOLIA’S TOP 100 COMPANIES
summary: Abstract Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting is an internationally standardized framework for assessing corporate sustainability, social responsibility, and long-term value creation. According to IBM, ESG represents an integrated framework for sustainability assessment. In Mongolia, formal regulation of ESG reporting was introduced in 2022 following the revision of the Regulation on Public Information Transparency by the Financial Regulatory Commission and the Mongolian Stock Exchange, which established mandatory disclosure requirements for ESG-related information for publicly listed companies. In parallel, the ESG Sustainability Reporting Guideline approved in 2022 has been undergoing alignment with the international IFRS S1 standard during 2024–2025. The objective of this study is to evaluate the current level of ESG disclosure among Mongolia’s TOP 100 companies as identified by the Mongolian National Chamber of Commerce and Industry in 2024. Of the TOP 100 companies, 25 firms that publicly disclosed ESG reports were selected for analysis. A total of 375 qualitative assessments were conducted across 15 indicators grouped into the three core ESG pillars—Environmental (E), Social (S), and Governance (G). Following qualitative scoring, company rankings and quantitative statistical analyses were performed using SPSS, including Ranking, One-way ANOVA, Welch and Brown–Forsythe robust tests, and post hoc comparisons. The One-way ANOVA results indicate no statistically significant differences in mean ESG scores across industry sectors (F(4,20)=0.98, p=.44). Levene’s test confirmed homogeneity of variances (p=.809), while the Welch (p=.65) and Brown–Forsythe (p=.49) robust tests similarly revealed no statistically significant inter-sectoral differences. Although the effect size (η²=.16) suggests a moderate practical effect, the absence of statistical significance may be attributable to the relatively small sample size and uneven distribution of firms across sectors. Post hoc analyses consistently grouped all sectors into a single homogeneous subset, further confirming the lack of statistically meaningful differences. The findings suggest that ESG reporting among Mongolia’s leading companies has not yet reached a level of sectoral differentiation, with systemic challenges related to data availability, reporting quality, and standard implementation remaining prevalent. Comparative analysis across ESG components shows that Environmental (E) disclosure scores highest, followed by Social (S) performance at a moderate level, while Governance (G) disclosure remains comparatively weak. As ESG reporting practices improve and data coverage expands, future research will enable more evidence-based assessments of sectoral policy implications, corporate governance quality, and social responsibility performance in Mongolia.

title: From Human Judgment to Machine Learning: A Philosophical Study of Knowledge Creation in Modern Accounting
summary: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning into accounting and auditing has transformed the creation, validation, and application of professional knowledge, raising questions about the legitimacy of algorithmic knowledge in accounting practice. Objective: This study examines the epistemological shift from human judgment to algorithmic knowledge in the implementation of Financial Accounting Standards (Standar Akuntansi Keuangan [SAK]) and Quality Management Systems (Sistem Manajemen Mutu [SMM]). Methods: This study employs a qualitative-interpretive approach through conceptual analysis and an examination of practitioners’ perspectives on the reliability, transparency, explainability, and trustworthiness of AI-assisted decision-making. Results: The results of the study show that AI can improve efficiency, predictive accuracy, and analytical capabilities in modern accounting practices but, at the same time, poses epistemological challenges in the form of limited algorithmic transparency, limited explainability, and the potential erosion of auditors’ professional skepticism. Although the conceptual analysis indicates that AI can positively affect efficiency and predictive accuracy, it also raises epistemic challenges related to transparency, accountability, and the preservation of professional skepticism. The shift from judgment-based knowledge to data-driven inferential knowledge has transformed the traditional epistemic authority held by accountants and auditors. The application of SAK and SMM in the accounting profession has implications for defining professional responsibilities in maintaining the quality of financial reporting and audit processes. Conclusion: This study proposes a human–machine epistemic partnership, in which AI functions as an analytical augmentation tool while accountants and auditors remain the primary epistemic authorities.

title: International Trade Policies and Sustainable Environmental Governance in Nigeria: A Legal Appraisal
summary: The intensification of global trade has increasingly positioned international trade law as a key instrument of environmental governance, extending its traditional commercial function to promote sustainability. This article critically examines the legal impact of international trade policies on sustainable environmental governance in Nigeria, whose economy remains heavily dependent on crude oil exports and other primary commodities. Adopting a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology, this evaluation assesses Nigeria's constitutional, statutory, and institutional frameworks in conjunction with multilateral trade agreements, regional trade instruments, and international environmental treaties, drawing comparative insights from the United Kingdom, the United States, and South Africa. The article argues that although Nigeria possesses an extensive legal and institutional framework for environmentally sustainable trade, its effectiveness is undermined by the non-justiciability of environmental obligations under Chapter II of the Constitution, weak regulatory enforcement, institutional fragmentation, and dependence on environmentally intensive exports. It further contends that legal scholarship has largely treated trade liberalisation and environmental protection as separate fields, overlooking the dual role of international trade law in both facilitating and constraining domestic environmental governance. Through doctrinal analysis of legislation, case law, and treaty provisions, supported by comparative institutional evaluation, the article demonstrates that Nigeria's principal challenge lies not in the absence of legal norms but in deficiencies in implementation and enforcement. It recommends constitutional recognition of enforceable environmental rights, integration of sustainability standards into trade and investment legislation, and strengthened regulatory institutions to align Nigeria's trade regime with evolving global environmental governance and sustainability requirements.

title: THE IMPACT OF GOOD CORPORATE GOVERNANCE, BOARD GENDER DIVERSITY AND OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY ON BANKING FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE
summary: This study is motivated by the fluctuating financial performance of banking companies in Indonesia during the research period. This condition reflects inconsistencies between the implementation of corporate governance, board gender diversity, and operational efficiency toward company profitability. This study aims to analyze the effect of Good Corporate Governance (GCG), Board Gender Diversity, and Operational Efficiency on financial performance proxied by Return on Assets (ROA). The research objects are banking companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the 2020–2024 period. This research employs a quantitative approach with an associative research design. The data used are secondary data obtained from companies’ financial statements and annual reports. The sample was determined using purposive sampling techniques, while the analytical method applied is panel data regression. The research testing includes selecting the best model, conducting classical assumption tests, and hypothesis testing. The results indicate that partially, Good Corporate Governance and Board Gender Diversity do not have a significant effect on Return on Assets (ROA). Meanwhile, Operational Efficiency has a significant effect on the financial performance of banking companies. Simultaneously, all independent variables significantly affect financial performance. The findings suggest that operational efficiency is the dominant factor in improving banking profitability. The implementation of corporate governance and board gender diversity still require optimization to provide a more substantial contribution to financial performance improvement.

title: Evaluating the Synergistic Impact of Digital Logistics Systems (eLMIS) and Financial Auditing (APTS) on Essential Commodity Availability in Ethiopian Public Healthcare Facilities: A Multilevel Analysis of the 2024/2025 National Survey
summary: Background: Chronic pharmaceutical stock outs hinder Universal Health Coverage in Ethiopia. To address this, the Ministry of Health introduced the electronic Logistics Management Information System for inventory visibility and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services for financial management. However, no national study has tested their combined impact. This study evaluated the individual and synergistic effects of electronic Logistics Management Information System and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services on essential commodity availability across Ethiopian public healthcare facilities. Methods; We conducted a secondary analysis of the 2024/2025 Ethiopian Service Provision Assessment dataset utilizing 1245 public facilities nested within 125 clusters. The primary outcome was optimal essential commodity availability (zero stock outs and 100% tracer commodity presence). A two-level mixed-effects logistic regression model with an interaction term evaluated synergy, reporting Adjusted Odds Ratios with 95% Confidence Intervals. Results; Overall optimal availability was 54.2% (95% CI; 51.4%–57.0%). Implementation rates were 41.2% for eLMIS, 38.2% for APTS and 26.5% for dual implementation. Facilities using eLMIS alone (AOR = 2.15; 95% CI: 1.52–3.04) and APTS alone (AOR = 1.82; 95% CI; 1.28–2.58) showed higher security. Dual implementation showed a profound synergistic effect (AOR = 4.32; 95% CI; 3.25–5.74, p < 0.001). Positive predictors included functional cold chains (AOR = 2.08), qualified staffing (AOR = 1.68), hub proximity (AOR = 1.58) and urban settings (AOR = 1.95). The model explained 66.2% of regional variance. Conclusion; Dual implementation of electronic Logistics Management Information System and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services creates a powerful synergistic impact on pharmaceutical availability. Synchronized national scale-up and cold chain investments are urgently needed to achieve supply chain resilience and Universal Health Coverage in Ethiopia.

title: El concepto contable de materialidad. Breve revisión en el caso de la información sobre tributos
summary: Actualmente, el concepto de materialidad resulta un eje central del debate sobre la responsabilidad social organizacional. Su significado varía según el marco conceptual y normativo que lo incluya, por lo que puede generar confusión en emisores y usuarios de reportes. Este ensayo analiza, comparativamente, distintos enfoques normativos de la materialidad a partir de los reportes financieros y sus repercusiones en el campo de la sostenibilidad. Se observan en los reportes de sostenibilidad dos enfoques divergentes: priorizar riesgos y oportunidades financieras o enfatizar los impactos sociales y ambientales. La normativa europea busca integrar estos dos enfoques bajo el concepto de “doble materialidad”. El trabajo ejemplifica la aplicación de estos enfoques en la información tributaria. En los reportes con enfoque financiero, la materialidad tributaria se centra en los efectos ciertos o contingentes sobre el patrimonio. En cambio, la materialidad de impacto considera también, entre otros, la planificación fiscal agresiva y la transparencia tributaria como factores relevantes. Las conclusiones subrayan la persistente ambigüedad en el contenido concreto del concepto de materialidad que dificulta la armonización entre los diversos reportes, tanto sean financieros como de sostenibilidad.

title: Evolución de la responsabilidad social corporativa en las pymes (2002-2025). Análisis bibliométrico y revisión crítica de un campo en consolidación
summary: This article examines the evolution of corporate social responsibility (CSR) in SMEs between 2002 and 2025 through a bibliometric analysis and a critical review of 1,343 articles indexed in Web of Science and Scopus. The trajectory of the field is organized into four stages - initial, take-off, consolidation, and expansion - and traces the shift from ethical approaches, centered on the owner-manager, toward strategic perspectives linked to sustainability, innovation, legitimacy, and performance, reinforced in recent years by ESG frameworks and the circular economy. The field now appears mature and interdisciplinary, although longitudinal and sector-specific studies remain scarce. Its application to SMEs in the art market is proposed as a future line of research.

title: Intelligent planning and scheduling system for supply chain logistics routes based on reinforcement learning
summary: The optimization of logistics routing and scheduling in supply chains is a critical challenge, particularly in dynamic environments characterized by fluctuating demand, traffic conditions, and stringent time-capacity constraints. Traditional optimization methods and heuristic-based approaches often struggle to adapt and maintain stability in non-stationary settings. Reinforcement learning models, while promising, face limitations in scalability, sensitivity to reward variance, and generalization under dynamic conditions. This research proposes the Dynamic Actor-Critic Proximal Policy Optimization (DACA-CPPO) framework to address these challenges. The Dynamic Actor-Critic algorithm (DACA) component improves policy and value adaptation by dynamically updating the actor and critic networks, while the Clipped Proximal Policy Optimization (CPPO) stabilizes policy updates through clipping, ensuring that the policy updates remain within a stable range and preventing large, destabilizing changes. The framework is evaluated using a dataset of 32,065 records with 26 features, split into 80% for training and 20% for testing. Data preprocessing techniques, including Z-score normalization and feasibility filtering, ensure consistent scaling and valid state transitions across training and testing sets. Node2Vec-based graph embeddings are employed to extract spatial and topological features of logistics networks, while statistical and temporal variables such as demand, capacity utilization, and scheduling urgency are incorporated into the state representation. The results show that the DACA-CPPO framework achieved 95% accuracy, reduced delivery costs, lowered delay rates, and improved route efficiency compared to baseline reinforcement learning strategies. Implemented in Python, the framework offers a stable, scalable, and adaptive solution for optimizing logistics planning in dynamic, real-time environments. Not applicable.

title: Drivers of blockchain technology adoption in construction supply chains: a systematic literature review and scientometric synthesis
summary: Purpose Blockchain technology (BT) has attracted growing attention in construction supply chain management (CSCM), yet existing research predominantly emphasises applications, technical architectures and barriers, providing limited understanding of the pressures motivating adoption. This study, therefore, systematically identifies and synthesises the drivers of BT adoption in construction supply chains (CSCs). Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review, conducted using the Scopus database, yielded 493 records. Following screening, 145 publications were retained for scientometric analysis, with 40 subsequently selected for qualitative content analysis. Findings The findings identify five interrelated driver themes: information governance; transactional and operational pressures; digital integration; sustainability and institutional pressures; and strategic and contextual pressures. Information fragmentation, limited visibility, trust and accountability deficits, coordination inefficiencies and unreliable provenance emerged as the most prominent motivations. However, driver salience varies across clients, contractors, subcontractors, suppliers, regulators and other supply-chain actors, demonstrating that adoption is a negotiated network-level decision rather than a uniform organisational response. Originality/value The findings provide a theoretically grounded basis for empirical research and help practitioners and policymakers align BT investments, governance arrangements and procurement interventions with clearly defined supply-chain problems rather than technology-led experimentation.

title: Making Shrimp in Moral Economies: Time, Ethics, and Labor in a Global Supply Chain
summary: ABSTRACT This article is part of the special issue 'Morality at Work: Ethnographies of Labor and Ethics' edited by Michael Vine and Sarah Winkler‐Reid. This article explores how future‐oriented temporalities shape people's labor experiences and ethical subjectivities within the global supply chain of brown shrimp. Drawing on ethnographic research with Dutch fishers, Moroccan shrimp peelers, and European processing managers, it traces how embedded notions of risk, luck, and destiny mediate workers' engagement with the uncertainty of the future. Processing company managers in Europe employ risk management practices to assert control over volatile markets, while North Sea fishers rely on notions of luck to navigate the unpredictability of fishing. In Moroccan peeling factories, workers often invoke destiny when making sense of their precarious working conditions. This article argues that attention to these divergent orientations toward the future offers critical insight into the moral economies that drive different forms of work under global capitalism.

title: Renewable Energy Output Uncertainty and Risk Transmission in Sustainable Power Supply Chains
summary: Uncertainty in renewable energy output changes how risk is allocated among generators and electricity retailers. We develop a mean–variance model with a thermal plant, a green plant, and a retailer under retailer-led Stackelberg and generation-side Cournot arrangements. In the Stackelberg arrangement, greater retailer risk aversion raises the purchase price and both outputs by compressing the retailer’s unit-margin exposure. In the Cournot arrangement, greater thermal-plant risk aversion lowers thermal and total output but raises green output, the expected purchase price, and renewable share. At the baseline endpoints, green share falls from 55.9% to 51.6% in the former arrangement and rises from 54.8% to 74.1% in the latter. The green plant’s optimal mean output is independent of its own risk coefficient under additive zero-skewness, quadratic-profit, and decision-independent uncertainty conditions; a skewed-shock counterexample shows where this shielding can fail. Local, global, and distributional sensitivity checks and 5000 feasible parameter draws reproduce the analytical directions while showing that magnitudes are calibration dependent. Because renewable share can move opposite to absolute renewable generation, sustainability assessment should report generation levels, shares, procurement prices, and risk allocation together. The model does not estimate emissions, welfare, or reliability.

title: ESG Pillar Composition and One-Year Accounting Loss Onset: Evidence from Bloomberg-Covered Firms, 2020–2024
summary: This study examines whether the internal composition of an environmental, social and governance (ESG) rating contains incremental information about one-year accounting-loss onset after the overall ESG level is held constant. Bloomberg environmental (E), social (S) and governance (G) pillar scores are reparameterised as ESGLevel = (E + S + G)/3, GovernanceHalo = G − (E + S)/2, and ESContrast = E − S. The FY2020–FY2024 panel contains 13,745 firm-years for 2751 relatively large listed firms; the principal model uses 8029 eligible transitions and 472 loss-onset events. A one-standard-deviation increase in GovernanceHalo has an average marginal effect of −0.02 percentage points (95% CI −0.87 to 0.83). Firm-blocked cross-validation provides essentially no incremental one-year predictive gain. Reviewer-driven sensitivity analyses using within-year standardised pillars, a firm fixed-effects linear probability model, Firth penalised logit, stabilised inverse-probability weighting for complete-case selection, and dynamic pre-trend controls do not reveal a stable loss-onset association. A separate 30% annual market-capitalisation contraction outcome is negatively associated with GovernanceHalo and remains significant after false-discovery-rate adjustment (q = 0.024), but it is a valuation-contraction proxy rather than an accounting-loss or crash-risk measure. The previously observed E/S score build-out is no longer evident after controls for prior score changes, current E/S level and historical score volatility. The evidence therefore rules out large average one-year loss-onset effects in this Bloomberg-covered sample while leaving open smaller, heterogeneous, longer-horizon and provider-specific effects.

title: Assessment of barriers to lean, green, and digital innovations in net-zero supply chain with an integrated MCDM approach
summary: Abstract Rapid industrialisation and increased online purchases have significantly increased the carbon footprint of supply chains (SCs), necessitating the transition towards net-zero SCs. Though lean, green, and digital (LGD) innovations have demonstrated potential to impact the net-zero SC transition, their adoption remains limited in emerging economies due to several barriers. Evaluation of the significance and interrelationships of the barriers remains elusive in the existing literature, highlighting the need for systematic investigation. Accordingly, this study aims to identify, evaluate, and prioritize the barriers to the adoption of LGD innovations in an emerging economy to facilitate the transition toward net-zero SCs. A systematic literature review was performed to identify barriers to incorporating LGD innovations, and principal component analysis with 345 respondents was employed to finalise the same. The finalised barriers were analysed using the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) methods in the Fermatean Fuzzy System (FFS) context. The outcomes suggest market competition (0.5641), the absence of a sustainable vision and goal (0.5489), the dilemma over the resilience of LGD innovations (0.5429), the absence of appropriate policy mechanisms (0.5418), and the lack of stakeholder support (0.5400) as the five most critical barriers. The study's implications could help SC practitioners make decisions related to net-zero emissions, potentially reducing adverse environmental impacts. The uniqueness of this work lies in the integration of FFS with AHP and DEMATEL to evaluate the barriers to integrating LGD innovations into SC activities.

title: Polarization in sustainability disclosure: the role of accounting structural deviation and its impact on firm value and audit fees
summary: Purpose This paper aims to investigate the financial consequences of sustainability disclosure polarization, conceptualized as the structural departure of a firm’s reporting practices from industry norms toward opposite extremes. It aims to determine how polarization impacts firm value and audit fees and to unpack the underlying mechanisms of uncertainty and the effectiveness of the audit committee (AC) in an emerging market region. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a quantitative approach, this study analyzes a panel dataset of 2,235 firm-year observations from listed companies across major ASEAN economies. Structural equation modeling is used to test a moderated-mediation framework. This methodology examines the complex pathways linking polarization to firm value and audit fees, accounting for country-specific heterogeneities and proxy sensitivity. Simultaneously, it assesses the contingent effects of uncertainty and AC effectiveness. Findings The results reveal a non-linear, inverted U-shaped relationship between the level of disclosure polarization and firm value, suggesting an optimal point of strategic differentiation exists. The study finds that disclosure polarization is positively associated with higher audit fees. These relationships are significantly mediated by environmental uncertainty, although these main effects exhibit conditionality across different national contexts within the region. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the AC is found to negatively moderate (weaken) the adverse impact of polarization on audit fees. Practical implications The findings offer actionable insights for managers to pursue an optimal, rather than maximal, disclosure strategy focused on quality to enhance firm value and control costs. For boards, it highlights the tangible financial benefit of investing in an effective AC. For ASEAN regulators, it suggests that policy should prioritize disclosure quality and comparability over mere quantity to foster market confidence. Originality/value By empirically operationalizing disclosure polarization through the structural deviation of reporting quality and governance from industry medians, this research moves beyond simplistic linear views of sustainability reporting. It contributes an integrated empirical model explaining both valuation and cost consequences through the dual lenses of external uncertainty and internal governance. The findings offer actionable insights for managers on optimizing disclosure quality and for regulators on fostering market confidence in emerging economies.

title: Post-pandemic strategic evaluation of food supply chains using hybrid decision models
summary: The increasing complexity and disruptions in global food supply chains (FSCs), particularly after COVID-19, have emphasized the need for resilient and adaptive strategies. This study conducts a comparative analysis of various FSC structures, such as Centralized, Decentralized, Digitalized, Localized, and Hybrid models. The comparison was carried out by applying two integrated multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods: Entropy-based MOORA and Entropy-based MARCOS. Objective weights for the eight criteria (cost, flexibility, resilience, lead time, sustainability, service level, innovation capability, and risk management) were assigned through the Entropy method that was used to reduce the subjective bias. In general, both methods identified the Digitalized and Hybrid supply chain models as the two highest-ranked alternatives, while the Centralized model ranked last. To make the findings even more robust, we carried out a sensitivity analysis where we changed the criterion weights in different scenarios. Moreover, an Entropy-based COPRAS method was employed for the robustness analysis, and the findings supported the stability and consistency of the rankings across different methodological approaches. By comparing two MCDM methods in a post-pandemic context, the study contributes to the literature while offering practical guidance for stakeholders on investing in digital infrastructure, adopting hybrid supply chain models, and integrating sustainability objectives into supply chain planning. The findings provide practical guidance for policymakers and executives seeking to enhance the resilience and environmental sustainability of FSCs amid global uncertainty.

title: Optimization of Sustainable Aviation Fuel Supply Chain from Macaúba Oil at the Regional Level
summary: This study analyzed the potential of macaúba (Acrocomia aculeata) for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production in Brazil, considering agricultural mapping, carbon balance, and economic optimization of the supply chain. About 17.6 million hectares of degraded pastures were found suitable for cultivation. The agricultural phase showed net negative emissions of –96.65 tCO2eq/ha, indicating significant climate mitigation potential. To meet the projected demand of 4.1 Mt/year of SAF by 2037, around 5.5 million hectares would be required, with Minas Gerais showing the highest productive potential. Economic viability depends on reducing raw material costs and valorizing co-products, with an estimated minimum selling price of USD 534/t of SAF.

title: Effect of Financial Attributes on Value of Listed Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
summary: The value of a firm remains a central concern in corporate finance because it reflects the overall wealth creation capacity of an organization and the perception of investors in the capital market. In the banking sector, firm value is particularly important due to its role in financial intermediation, economic stability, and investor confidence. This study examined the effect of financial attributes on the value of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria. The study focused on profitability, liquidity, leverage, capital adequacy, and asset quality as key financial attributes influencing firm value. The study adopted an ex-post facto research design, and secondary data were obtained from the annual reports and audited financial statements of 14 listed deposit money banks on the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX), as well as NGX fact books, covering the period from 2016 to 2024. Panel regression analysis was employed as a technique of data analysis. The results revealed that profitability, capital adequacy, and asset quality have positive and statistically significant effects on firm value (Tobin’s Q), while liquidity and leverage show negative but statistically insignificant relationships with firm value. The study concludes that financial strength indicators play a critical role in enhancing firm value and recommends that bank management focus on improving profitability, strengthening capital adequacy, and enhancing asset quality to sustain market valuation and investor confidence.

title: Anchoring in the Storm: How Does Digital Intelligence Technology Foster Green Innovation Resilience?
summary: Abstract In an era characterized by dual transformations and climate-induced turbulence, manufacturing firms are compelled to shift their strategic paradigm from static "green growth" to dynamic "green survival." Based on data from Chinese A-share manufacturing listed companies from 2012 to 2023, this study empirically examines the impact mechanisms and boundary conditions of digital intelligence technology on green innovation resilience. The findings indicate that: (1) Digital intelligence technology significantly enhances the green innovation resilience of manufacturing firms. (2) Mechanism tests reveal that digital intelligence technology empowers green innovation resilience through a dual pathway of alleviating financing constraints and improving managerial efficiency. (3) Climate risk attention plays a critical moderating role in this process; specifically, it significantly enhances the marginal contributions of financing constraint alleviation and managerial efficiency improvement to green innovation resilience. (4) Heterogeneity analysis shows that the empowering effect is more pronounced in non-high-tech, non-heavy-polluting, and high-competition industries, as well as in Eastern-based, non-labor-intensive, and upstream firms. This study reveals that only by achieving strategic alignment between digital capabilities and subjective risk perception can firms effectively coordinate resources to maintain green innovation resilience.

title: Flow‐Driven ESG Returns
summary: ABSTRACT I show that the recent returns to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing are strongly driven by price impact from flows toward ESG portfolios. Using data on trades, I estimate the market's ability to accommodate ESG flows, which is given by the elasticity of substitution between ESG and other stocks. I show that every dollar flowing toward a representative ESG portfolio increases the market value of ESG stocks by $0.8. The growing institutional flows into the ESG portfolio are the main driver of ESG returns and have caused an annual flow‐driven return of 1.9%. In the absence of flows, ESG stocks would not have outperformed the market from 2012 to 2023.

title: Blockchain Management Empowering Green and Climate Finance: Mechanisms, Real‑World Dilemmas and Optimization Paths
summary: Against the background of China's dual-carbon strategic goals, green and climate finance have achieved rapid scale expansion as critical instruments for low-carbon economic transition. Nevertheless, the whole market is still plagued by prominent governance risks, including intentional environmental data manipulation, and repeated double-counting of carbon assets, as well as poor traceability of green project capital flows. As an innovative trust-rebuilding management paradigm rather than simple technical tools, blockchain management leverages distributed ledgers, data immutability and smart-contract functions to deliver credible technical support for green-climate finance. This paper adopts qualitative analytical research, including literature review and dual-case comparison, to investigate how blockchain management functions within green credit, carbon trading and green bond scenarios. It identifies major practical obstacles and puts forward coordinated institutional-technical optimization proposals. The study reveals that blockchain can effectively mitigate information asymmetry in green-financial practice. Nevertheless, its large-scale commercial deployment is hindered by on-chain-off-chain data fragmentation, insufficient unified regulatory standards and relatively high technical operation costs. Therefore, collaborative governance mechanisms, unified industry-wide standards and lower access thresholds for small- and medium-sized enterprises are urgently required for future development.

title: Corporate Governance, Leverage, and Working Capital Turnover as Predictors of Financial Health in Indonesian Logistics and Transportation Companies
summary: Background: Financial vulnerability remains important in capital-intensive logistics and transportation companies during periods of disruption and recovery. Objective: This study examines the associations of leverage, Working Capital Turnover, and institutional ownership, used as a corporate governance proxy, with the financial health of Indonesian logistics and transportation companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange. Methods: A balanced panel of 75 firm-year observations from 15 companies during 2020–2024 was analyzed using Pooled OLS, Fixed Effects, and Random Effects estimators. Model selection was guided by the Chow, Breusch–Pagan Lagrange multiplier, and Hausman tests. Results: The Random Effects model was selected. Leverage was not significantly associated with the Altman Z-Score (β = 1.32, p = 0.294), so H1 was not supported. Working Capital Turnover had a significant negative association (β = −0.076, p = 0.021); because this direction contradicted the positive hypothesis and the ratio contained extreme values linked to negative working capital, H2 was not supported. Institutional ownership had the strongest significant positive association among the predictors in the selected model (β = 25.60, p < 0.001), supporting H3. Conclusion: Institutional ownership is positively associated with financial health, while the WCTO result requires cautious interpretation because of its denominator structure and overlap between the predictors and components of the Altman Z-Score.

title: Mekari Jurnal: Accounting Software Utilizing Artificial Intelligence Technology
summary: Mekari Jurnal is a cloud-based accounting and financial management software platform that utilizes artificial intelligence (AI) technology to help businesses manage financial processes in a more integrated way. The platform brings essential accounting activities into one system, including bookkeeping, transaction recording, invoicing, accounts receivable, expense management, inventory management, bank reconciliation, taxation, and financial reporting. Through automation and data integration, Mekari Jurnal helps businesses reduce manual accounting processes while providing better visibility into financial data. Its combination of accounting software, cloud technology, automation, and AI supports more efficient and structured financial workflows. Mekari Jurnal is designed for businesses across different sizes and industries in Indonesia that need an integrated solution for managing financial information and accounting processes as their operations grow. title: Layering of Controls: MCS Transformation in a Hybrid Public Accounting Firm
summary: Background: This study introduces layering of controls as a longitudinal and cumulative pattern in the transformation of Management Control Systems (MCS) within professional service firms. Objective: Unlike redesign or archetype-change perspectives, which treat MCS transformation as substitutive, this research demonstrates how new controls accumulate without replacing existing ones. The study draws on a single-case, longitudinal investigation of a non-Big Four Indonesian public accounting firm affiliated with a global network, observed across nearly four decades of organizational growth. Methods: Methodologically, the research combines eight years of participant observation by an insider partner-researcher (2017–2025), semi-structured interviews with six purposively selected informants reflecting maximum variation across hierarchy and background, and analysis of organizational documents, with reflexivity and triangulation employed to mitigate insider bias. Results: The findings reveal four sequential layers: founder-based personal and cultural controls, action controls through global audit methodology, formal governance, and integrated audit technology. Each layer reinforces rather than supplants the preceding layers. Conclusion: The study contributes by extending the MCS-as-package framework with a temporal dimension, explaining how intrinsic motivation sustains cultural control in professional firms, and showing that global affiliation in a hybrid model strengthens, rather than erodes, local strategic authority in emerging-market audit firms.

title: The Mediating Role of Green Supply Chain Management between Lean Manufacturing Practices and Sustainable Performance
summary: The Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA)-registered multinational manufacturing companies in Laguna continue to face financial, social, and sustainability challenges despite adopting Lean Manufacturing Practices (LMP). However, evidence remains limited on how Green Supply Chain Management (GSCM) enhances the sustainability outcomes of lean initiatives in the Philippine manufacturing context. This study examined GSCM's mediating role in the relationship between LMP and Sustainable Performance (SP) among PEZA-registered multinational manufacturing companies in Laguna. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design, data were collected from middle- to upper-level managers through a researcher-made questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics, regression analysis, and mediation analysis. The findings revealed that selected LMP dimensions significantly influenced SP, while GSCM significantly mediated the effects of selected LMP on financial, social and environmental performance. The results indicate that environmentally responsible supply chain practices can serve as an important pathway linking selected lean manufacturing practices with sustainable performance. Based on these findings, the study proposed a strategic plan to help PEZA promote sustainable manufacturing practices and enhance the competitiveness of multinational manufacturing companies. The study provides empirical evidence that integrating lean and green practices is essential to achieving long-term sustainable performance and advancing the Philippines’ goal of becoming a leading sustainable manufacturing hub in Asia.

title: Traditional Meat Supply Chain Challenges in Nepal: An Independent Field Study and Applied Business Case
summary: This independent research report examines meat and poultry supply-chain challenges across multiple ecological and commercial regions of Nepal, based on approximately two months of exploratory field observation conducted in 2022. The study considers differences in livestock market access, transportation, intermediary structures, sanitation and freshness expectations, customer purchasing patterns, and commercial demand across mountain, hill, and Terai/Inner-Terai settings. The report also presents an applied business case based on Aachano Meats, a meat-processing and distribution venture subsequently co-founded in Bharatpur. The case examines the practical implementation of a localized supply-chain model connecting poultry suppliers and smaller producers with centralized processing, demand-based distribution, five retail locations, local delivery, B2B customers, and a cold-storage pilot. The findings suggest that a key operational challenge was not simply the presence of intermediaries, but fragmentation between production, processing, demand information, distribution, and customer requirements. The applied case demonstrates how centralized upstream processing combined with localized distribution and final retail preparation can be used to address some of these coordination challenges. This work is an exploratory independent field study and applied case study. It was not conducted using a statistically representative national sample and should not be interpreted as a national survey of Nepal's meat industry.

title: When a security update stops the world: The CrowdStrike Falcon outage and the fragility of the digital supply chain
summary: This teaching case examines the global information technology outage of 19 July 2024, when a defective content update to CrowdStrike’s Falcon endpoint security platform crashed approximately 8.5 million Microsoft Windows devices and disrupted airlines, hospitals, banks, broadcasters and emergency services around the world. Unlike most prominent information security cases, no attacker was involved: the incident was caused by the very software organisations had deployed to protect themselves. The case therefore shifts attention from confidentiality-centred views of security towards availability, operational resilience and the governance of digital supply chains. We first discuss the concentration of risk created by modern software supply chains and the trade-offs inherent in security tooling that operates inside the operating system kernel. We then introduce a business model perspective to show how a single quality failure propagated through the value propositions, value chains and revenue models of both the vendor and its customers. Finally, we describe the incident, its technical root causes and its aftermath, including an estimated multi-billion-dollar economic impact, congressional scrutiny, and litigation between Delta Air Lines and CrowdStrike. The case enables students to analyse third-party risk, software deployment practices, crisis response and the regulatory implications of concentrated digital dependence.

title: Resolving Manufacturing's Digital Transformation Paradox via Configurational Legitimacy-Dependencies Alignment
summary: This study addresses the digital transformation paradox by examining how configurations of institutional pressures and resource dependencies determine the performance of different digital transformation models. Integrating institutional theory and resource dependence theory within a configurational framework, the authors employ a hybrid fsQCA-NCA analysis of large listed manufacturing firms. Results reveal multiple equifinal paths to high performance, demonstrating substitutive and compensatory relationships between external legitimacy and internal capabilities. The primary contribution is a theoretically grounded “Legitimacy-Dependency Alignment Matrix” that offers managers a diagnostic tool for strategic decision-making. They advance beyond linear explanations by showing that strategic alignment—not isolated factors—explains digital transformation outcomes.

title: STRATEGIC DIRECTIONS FOR MODERNIZING CREDIT SERVICES IN COMMERCIAL BANKS UNDER DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
summary: In the context of rapid digital transformation, modernizing commercial bank credit services has become a strategic priority. This article examines key directions for reforming credit mechanisms through digital technologies and data-driven solutions, aiming to optimize lending processes, reduce operational costs, and improve customer experience. Particular attention is given to Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Big Data analytics in automated credit scoring and risk assessment. The study also analyzes end-to-end digital lending channels, open banking APIs for real-time decision-making, and the potential of blockchain and smart contracts to enhance transparency and security. Key challenges, including cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, and data privacy, are discussed alongside practical solutions. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations to strengthen banks' competitiveness, improve credit portfolio quality, and expand financial inclusion.

title: The Digital Transformation Dilemma: Institutional Barriers to Scaling Agile in Public and Corporate Sectors
summary: Digital transformation of public and corporate sectors implies the adoption of Agile methodologies to enhance adaptability and customer centricity. However, scaling Agile in large organizations and government agencies frequently fails to meet anticipated outcomes; while bureaucratic overhead escalates, innovation activity declines and institutional conflicts emerge. This study aims to identify recurrent patterns of institutional failure in Agile scaling and to construct a conceptual model of the strategic dilemma arising from regulatory constraints and bureaucratic culture. The methodology is based on multiple case studies of six publicly documented cases from the financial, IT, manufacturing, and public sectors. Crosscase analysis has revealed three patterns: imitation of transformation while preserving the bureaucratic core, conflict between team autonomy and centralized control, and the cultural immunity of the bureaucratic environment. The study has identified three interrelated mechanisms: the coordination costs escalation, the hollowing out of values (institutional rigidity), and contextual rejection. These mechanisms produce a cumulative lock-in effect that undermines the strategic potential of Agile. The scientific novelty lies in the transition from an isolated enumeration of success factors to a model of cumulative interaction among institutional barriers, which is demonstrated through a comparative analysis of international and Russian cases. The practical significance consists in diagnostic questions designed to help organizations identify risks arising from the strategic dilemma and transition towards informed hybrid project management models.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF UZBEKISTAN'S FOREIGN TRADE AND THE EFFECTIVENESS OF PROSPECTS FOR INTEGRATION INTO INTERNATIONAL MARKETS
summary: This thesis examines the digital transformation of Uzbekistan's foreign trade, the electronic modernization of customs and logistics processes, and the prospects for deeper integration into international markets. The study analyzes foreign-trade dynamics in 2021-2025 and assesses the channels through which digital customs infrastructure, data exchange, electronic declarations, automated risk management, and e-logistics can improve trade efficiency. According to national statistics, Uzbekistan's foreign trade turnover increased from USD 42.2 billion in 2021 to USD 82.8 billion in 2025 [1]. Although this growth cannot be attributed to digitalization alone, reduced document-processing time, faster customs clearance, and integration of logistics information systems are important factors in lowering transaction costs [4; 5]. The paper proposes aligning digital trade infrastructure with international standards, widening SME access to export platforms, strengthening cross-border data exchange, and coordinating these reforms with Uzbekistan's WTO accession process [3; 6].

title: From AI Readiness to Productivity: The Role of Innovation Capacity in Europe's Digital Transformation
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly expected to enhance productivity, yet technological adoption alone may be insufficient to generate measurable economic gains. This study examines how AI and digital readiness are associated with productivity across European economies and whether this relationship operates through innovation capacity and human capital. Using a balanced dataset covering the EU-27 in 2021, 2023, and 2024, we estimate a Partial Least Squares Path Modelling (PLS-PM) model linking AI/Digital Readiness, Innovation Capacity, Human Capital, Productivity, and Inclusive Growth, with country-cluster bootstrap inference. The results indicate an indirect-only mediation pattern: AI/Digital Readiness is strongly associated with Innovation Capacity but has no significant direct relationship with Productivity, whereas Innovation Capacity is strongly associated with Productivity and generates a significant indirect effect. Human Capital neither mediates nor moderates this relationship, and Productivity is not significantly associated with Inclusive Growth. The innovation-mediated pathway remains significant across several alternative specifications, although it becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero when business R&D expenditure is excluded from Innovation Capacity. Leave-one-country-out cross-validation also indicates substantial predictive relevance for Productivity. Overall, the findings suggest that the relationship between digital readiness and productivity in European economies is closely associated with the innovation capabilities through which technological opportunities can be translated into economic value.

title: The stabilizing effect of intelligent manufacturing policy on supply chains: analysis from the new energy vehicle industry
summary: Purpose In the context of global value chain restructuring, intensifying industrial competition, and rapid technological change, the role of intelligent manufacturing in shaping supply chain stability has become an important issue in industrial strategy and operations management. This study aims to investigate whether and how intelligent manufacturing pilot policies enhance supply chain stability under global uncertainties. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on socio-technical systems theory and the perspective of technological sovereignty, this study employs a difference-in-differences model based on data from listed firms in China's A-share new energy vehicle industry from 2010 to 2024 to examine the stabilizing effects of intelligent manufacturing pilots. Findings Intelligent manufacturing pilot policies significantly enhance supply chain stability by reducing supplier volatility and customer volatility. This effect is positively moderated by diversification breakthrough, information flow facilitation, and physical flow optimization. The stabilizing effect is more pronounced among firms with stronger demand for cross-boundary innovation and higher levels of supply-demand uncertainty. Originality/value This study integrates socio-technical systems theory and technological sovereignty, offering new insights into how intelligent technologies reshape supply chain stability amid global value chain restructuring.

title: Supply Chain Readiness and Food Security in Dryland Environments: Empirical Evidence from Kenya’s Arid and Semi-Arid Land Counties
summary: Agri-food distribution networks operating across dryland regions face intense operational disruptions caused by extreme climate shocks, infrastructural vulnerabilities, and rapid market fluctuations. This study examines the empirical effect of Supply Chain Readiness Strategy on food security outcomes across Kenya’s 29 Arid and Semi-Arid Land (ASAL) counties. Theoretical anchoring is established through Dynamic Capability Theory (DCT)—specifically focusing on sensing and seizing capabilities—and Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) Theory. Supply chain readiness was operationalised through three key indicators: early-warning surveillance systems, pre-formulated emergency response protocols, and rapid logistics mobilisation capabilities. Utilising an explanatory cross-sectional survey design grounded in a pragmatic philosophical framework, primary empirical data were collected from a census of County Directors of Agriculture and Crop Production Officers (N=29; 100% response rate). Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was conducted for data reduction, extracting a single dominant component that accounted for 81.20% of total variance. Binary logistic regression and marginal effects estimations were employed to test the underlying hypothesis. Empirical findings revealed that supply chain readiness exerts a statistically significant positive effect on food security (β= 1.624, p = 0.028). The calculated odds ratio (β= 5.073) demonstrates that ASAL counties with structured readiness strategies are over five times more likely to maintain stable food security conditions than those with low readiness capabilities. Marginal effects estimation showed that a unit increase in readiness increases the probability of achieving food security by 25.1 percentage points (dy/dx = 0.251, p = 0.032). The study concludes that proactive early-warning surveillance, pre-allocated emergency funds, and rapid deployment protocols are essential drivers of food availability and market stability in volatile dryland ecosystems. Devolved county governments and humanitarian agencies are urged to institutionalise predictive surveillance systems and pre-approved logistics contingency frameworks.

title: The Procurement Professional in the AI Era: Procurement Capability under Technological Change and Strategic Supply Uncertainty
summary: This independent professional research paper examines whether established procurement competency frameworks sufficiently articulate the capabilities required of practitioners operating in an environment shaped by artificial intelligence, changing international trade relationships and strategic supply uncertainty. Using a comparative analysis of the Government of Canada's Procurement Community Competencies and the United Kingdom's Government Commercial Function People Standards, the paper identifies areas in which existing professional standards may benefit from more explicit, observable and assessable behaviours. The research proposes a three-part capability architecture that retains established procurement competencies while introducing seven AI-related practice areas and four wider strategic practice areas. These address AI-supported decision-making, governance, evidence verification, trade and policy interpretation, supply-chain resilience, public-value trade-offs and integrated commercial judgement. An Ontario procurement-policy case study illustrates how these capabilities may be applied within a provincial environment. The paper also considers transferability across Canadian jurisdictions, recognising differences in legislation, trade obligations, policy requirements and institutional governance. A worked procurement decision exercise, proposed assessment criteria and an independent validation methodology provide a practical basis for professional discussion and future pilot testing. The proposed framework has not yet been empirically validated. Related publication This research builds upon the professional-development architecture explored in Rajbinder Kaur's book, The Procurement Professional: A Career Guide for the AI Era (2026). The book provides a structured learning pathway across procurement practice, commercial judgement, leadership, risk, resilience and digital transformation, while the research paper examines how those capabilities may be articulated and assessed in contemporary procurement environments. title: Building Africa's Digital & AI Foundation: Data Infrastructure & Trust
summary: Building Africa's Digital Foundation: Data, Infrastructure and Trust is the inaugural whitepaper in a thought leadership series exploring the forces shaping Africa's digital and artificial intelligence future. Written from the perspective of a telecommunications and data transformation leader, the paper argues that Africa's next era of economic growth will be built on the strategic combination of digital infrastructure, data, and trust. Drawing on examples from Ghana and across the African continent, the paper examines how connectivity, cloud platforms, digital identity systems, fintech innovation, artificial intelligence, and modern data ecosystems are becoming the foundational layers of a new digital economy. Positioned at the intersection of technology, business strategy, and public policy, the paper presents a framework for policymakers, business executives, technology leaders, and development practitioners seeking to accelerate digital transformation while ensuring that growth remains inclusive, ethical, and economically meaningful. As the first publication in a broader series, Leading Africa's Digital & AI Future, it establishes the central thesis that Africa's digital future will be determined not only by the technologies it adopts, but by the institutions, governance structures, talent ecosystems, and trust frameworks it builds around them. Subsequent papers expand on these themes by examining the evolution from digital foundations to data intelligence, artificial intelligence, digital leadership, and the future of value creation in African organizations.

title: Navigating the Digital Transformation of Islamic Education: Authority, Verification, and the Problem of Unsourced Religious Content
summary: Digital platforms have become a primary route through which Indonesian students encounter religious knowledge, and teachers of Islamic education increasingly meet classroom questions whose answers students have already obtained from sources carrying no chain of transmission. This study examines how the digital transformation of Islamic education reconfigures the relationship between teacher, text, and learner, and asks what verification practice becomes possible when the volume of accessible religious content exceeds any teacher’s capacity to authenticate it. The study is a conceptual synthesis of peer-reviewed literature, policy documents, and institutional reports, selected purposively and analysed thematically across accessibility, content authenticity, pedagogical innovation, teacher role, ethics, and institutional readiness. The analysis finds that digitalisation expands access decisively but redistributes interpretive authority in ways existing teacher preparation does not address; that content generated by artificial intelligence intensifies rather than creates this problem, since fluency without sanad is already characteristic of much online religious material; and that blended learning models developed for school-age learners transfer poorly to the adult and para-professional audiences that dominate Islamic non-formal education without andragogical adjustment. The study argues that the practical task facing institutions is not the adoption of technology but the design of verification competence, and proposes three design principles: teaching provenance rather than conclusions, making the limits of teacher authority explicit, and building institutional review of digital content into curriculum governance rather than leaving it to individual discretion.

title: The use of artificial intelligence and big data in the Islamic FinTech ecosystem: opportunities, risks and a governance perspective
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine Islamic FinTech transformation as a governance process, not only as a source of technical efficiency. Although previous research emphasizes growth, it gives less attention to how artificial intelligence and big data affect the field’s ethical and institutional foundations. The study therefore considers how these technologies influence Sharīʿah compliance, ethical governance and institutional legitimacy. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a critical narrative review of peer-reviewed publications and selected scholarly and institutional sources. The main search assessed 120 distinct candidate records and included 87 in the analytical synthesis. A separate complementary update and re-evaluation assessed 68 records, used 20 and excluded 48. Hybrid inductive–deductive coding produced seven constructs and four cross-cutting analytical dimensions; the relationships proposed are empirically testable theoretical propositions, not causal findings. Findings Algorithmic transparency, ethical principles, digital Sharīʿah auditing and data privacy are central to institutional trust, continued Sharīʿah compliance and legitimacy. The framework organizes seven constructs across five relational stages, with algorithmic transparency as a possible mediator between technological inputs and institutional trust. Trust functions as the legitimacy mechanism, sustainability as the final outcome, and a feedback loop connects institutional learning and regulatory alignment. Originality/value Unlike reviews that mainly catalogue applications, adoption drivers or performance effects, this study explains how technological inputs may acquire legitimacy through ethical governance, Sharīʿah compliance and algorithmic transparency. The resulting framework connects institutional trust with sustainability and translates unresolved relationships into a testable research agenda.

title: Mekari Jurnal: AI-Powered Accounting Software for Modern Businesses
summary: Managing business finances involves more than recording income and expenses. Transaction data, invoices, inventory, payments, taxes, and financial reports need to be connected so businesses can gain a more comprehensive view of their financial condition. Integrated Accounting and Financial Management Mekari Jurnal is a cloud-based accounting and financial management software platform that utilizes artificial intelligence (AI) technology to support businesses in managing their financial processes. The platform brings key accounting and financial activities together within an integrated system. Businesses can use Mekari Jurnal to manage bookkeeping, record transactions, handle invoices and accounts receivable, monitor expenses, manage inventory, perform bank reconciliation, manage tax-related processes, and generate financial reports based on recorded operational data. Supporting Accounting Automation with AI AI technology can support accounting workflows by helping businesses reduce repetitive manual processes and process financial data more efficiently. Combined with automation and cloud-based access, this approach allows financial information to be managed in a more structured and connected environment. Mekari Jurnal combines accounting software capabilities with AI technology and financial data integration to support more efficient accounting workflows. This can help businesses reduce reliance on manual processes while maintaining better visibility into their financial information. Building Scalable Financial Processes As businesses grow, financial data and accounting activities can become increasingly complex. An integrated accounting system can help businesses organize financial processes while making relevant information easier to monitor and use for reporting. By combining cloud technology, accounting automation, integrated financial data, and AI capabilities, Mekari Jurnal supports businesses in building more structured and scalable financial management processes.
